questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 68-year-old client is 1 day postoperative after a bowel resection. The client has become short-tempered with staff and says, “I’m just worn out.” The daughter says, “He always gets grumpy in hospitals.” SpO₂ is 90% on room air (96% on admission), RR 22/min, HR 98/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Assess breath sounds and work of breathing, and apply oxygen per protocol
Coach the client to use the incentive spirometer 10 times every hour
Notify the provider about the change in the client’s mood and behavior
Recheck the SpO₂ with a new probe placed on a warm, well-perfused finger
optionRationales: Correct. Irritability and fatigue with a falling SpO₂ are early signs of impaired oxygenation, so the nurse assesses and supports oxygenation before blaming mood.
Incorrect. Incentive spirometry helps prevent atelectasis, but it is a preventive measure; a falling SpO₂ needs assessment and oxygen support now.
Incorrect. The provider will need to know, but the nurse first assesses the lungs and starts protocol oxygen so the report includes complete data.
Incorrect. Ruling out a probe error is reasonable, but the rising respiratory rate and heart rate already confirm a real change, and rechecking delays care.
questions.rationale: Mild impairments in oxygenation cause vague symptoms — fatigue, irritability, and discomfort — that are easy to write off as personality or hospital stress. Here the behavior change arrives together with an SpO₂ drop from 96% to 90% and a rising respiratory rate, which points to developing hypoxemia (for example, from postoperative atelectasis). The nurse assesses the respiratory system and supports oxygenation per protocol before accepting a non-physiologic explanation. Rechecking the probe or calling the provider is tempting, but the supporting signs already confirm the change, and the nurse acts on it first.
questions.takeaway: New irritability or fatigue plus a falling SpO₂ is an oxygenation problem until proven otherwise.
questions.hintContent: Compare today’s SpO₂ with the admission value, then recall which vague symptoms mild hypoxemia produces.
questions.hintStrategy: When a family’s explanation competes with a physiologic cue, rule out the physiologic cause first.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: At the start of the shift, a nurse on a medical unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with COPD who has a barrel chest and clubbed fingers at baseline
A client with asthma who speaks in full sentences with an SpO₂ of 96%
A client with cellulitis who has new neck muscle use and unequal chest rise
A client with pneumonia who has right lower lobe crackles and a low fever
optionRationales: Incorrect. Barrel chest and clubbing are long-standing findings, not new changes in this client’s condition.
Incorrect. Full sentences and a normal SpO₂ show this client is moving air well and is currently stable.
Correct. Breathing is normally effortless and symmetric, so new accessory muscle use with asymmetric chest rise is an acute change that needs immediate assessment.
Incorrect. Crackles and a low-grade fever need monitoring, but they are expected with pneumonia; new neck muscle use with unequal chest rise is an acute change.
questions.rationale: Breathing is autonomic, so a sudden change in how a person breathes means something in the body has changed and must be addressed immediately. In a healthy person the neck muscles stay relaxed and the chest rises and falls equally, so new accessory muscle use plus unequal chest rise in a client admitted for a skin infection is unexpected and possibly an acute lung collapse. The COPD client’s barrel chest and clubbing look dramatic, which is why they tempt students, but they are chronic, baseline findings. Acute and unexpected outranks chronic and expected.
questions.takeaway: A new change in breathing effort or symmetry outranks dramatic but chronic findings.
questions.hintContent: Sort each finding into “new” versus “baseline or expected for age.”
questions.hintStrategy: Acute and unexpected beats chronic and expected when choosing whom to see first.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: Two days after a cesarean birth, a 31-year-old client suddenly reports shortness of breath and says, “I feel like something terrible is happening.” RR 32/min, HR 128/min, SpO₂ 87% on room air. Breath sounds are clear and equal, and chest expansion is symmetric. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Coach incentive spirometry to reexpand collapsed alveoli
Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen per protocol
Assess the calves for redness, warmth, and swelling
Ask the AP to obtain a complete set of vital signs
optionRationales: Incorrect. Clear, equal breath sounds argue against atelectasis, so this treats an airflow problem the client does not appear to have.
Correct. Sudden hypoxemia with clear lungs suggests blocked pulmonary blood flow; supporting oxygenation now, then notifying the provider, comes first.
Incorrect. Calf findings can support a suspected clot, but the client is already hypoxemic, and more assessment delays oxygen and positioning.
Incorrect. Vital signs are already known; delegating delays action for an unstable client.
questions.rationale: When hypoxemia appears suddenly but air is clearly moving in — clear breath sounds and symmetric expansion — think of the perfusion side of the V/Q match: fresh air reaches the alveoli, but a clot blocks blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries. Postpartum and postoperative clients are at risk. The nurse stays with the client, raises the head of the bed, applies oxygen per protocol, and notifies the provider immediately. Incentive spirometry is tempting because it is routine after surgery, but it treats a ventilation problem the assessment does not support.
questions.takeaway: Sudden hypoxemia with clear lungs points to blocked blood flow — support oxygenation and call the provider.
questions.hintContent: Clear, equal breath sounds tell you air is getting in; ask what else keeps oxygen from reaching the blood.
questions.hintStrategy: For an unstable client, pick the action that supports oxygenation now over routine or delegated tasks.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: After a motorcycle crash, a 22-year-old client is brought to the emergency department with a suspected pelvic fracture. The client is newly confused and keeps asking where they are. HR 132/min, BP 84/50 mm Hg, RR 28/min, SpO₂ 98% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. Which action is most important for the nurse to take?
options: Increase the oxygen flow to 6 L/min to bring the SpO₂ up to 100%
Request an arterial blood gas to check the oxygen level
Reorient the client and raise the side rails for safety
Report signs of hemorrhage and prepare for blood replacement
optionRationales: Incorrect. The hemoglobin that remains is already saturated; more oxygen cannot make up for missing carriers.
Incorrect. An ABG gives more data on oxygenation, but the SpO₂ is already normal; the problem is too few oxygen carriers from bleeding.
Incorrect. Safety measures are appropriate for a confused client, but the confusion is a sign of shock, and treating its cause comes first.
Correct. Confusion, tachycardia, and hypotension with a normal SpO₂ suggest too little hemoglobin to carry oxygen; replacing blood treats the cause.
questions.rationale: Most oxygen in the blood rides on hemoglobin, so oxygen delivery depends on having enough hemoglobin as well as on ventilation. A pulse oximeter only shows the percentage of the hemoglobin present that is carrying oxygen; in a bleeding client that percentage stays high while the total oxygen delivered falls. New confusion (the brain is sensitive to low oxygen), tachycardia, and hypotension reveal tissue hypoxia despite an SpO₂ of 98%. Turning up the oxygen is the tempting choice, but it cannot fix a shortage of carriers — restoring blood volume and hemoglobin does.
questions.takeaway: A normal SpO₂ cannot rule out tissue hypoxia when hemoglobin is being lost.
questions.hintContent: Ask what a pulse oximeter actually measures and what it cannot measure.
questions.hintStrategy: When the monitor and the client disagree, treat the client and the underlying cause.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An assistive personnel (AP) reports that a 2-month-old infant’s respiratory rate is 68/min, counted for 15 seconds and multiplied by 4. The infant is feeding well, has pink lips, and has no retractions. Which action should the RN take first?
options: Notify the provider that the infant has developed new tachypnea
Document the rate and recount it at the next scheduled check
Recount the respirations for a full 60 seconds while the infant is quiet
Apply blow-by oxygen near the infant’s face during the feeding
optionRationales: Incorrect. The value may be inaccurate; the RN confirms the finding before escalating for a stable-appearing infant.
Incorrect. Planning a recount is reasonable, but documenting data the RN knows may be inaccurate is premature; the RN verifies the rate now.
Correct. Infant breathing is often irregular, so the RN verifies the rate with a full-minute count before acting on it.
Incorrect. The infant shows no distress, and oxygen is not indicated on the basis of an unverified number.
questions.rationale: Newborns and infants normally breathe 30–60 times per minute, and their pattern is often irregular with brief pauses. A 15-second count multiplied by 4 can easily exaggerate or miss those pauses, so respirations in infants and young children are counted for a full 60 seconds. Because the infant is pink, feeding, and free of retractions, there is no emergency that justifies acting before verifying. Notifying the provider is tempting because 68 is above the range, but the RN first obtains accurate data; if the full count is still high, the RN escalates.
questions.takeaway: Count an infant’s respirations for a full minute before acting on an abnormal rate.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal infant rate and why a short count is unreliable at this age.
questions.hintStrategy: In a stable client, “assess before you act” — verify questionable data before escalating.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: An 81-year-old client with heart failure is receiving IV fluids at 150 mL/h for dehydration. Four hours later the client is dyspneic, with fine crackles in both lungs, RR 28/min, and an SpO₂ of 89% (97% at the start of the infusion). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Sit the client upright and slow the infusion to a keep-open rate
Encourage coughing to move secretions out of the large airways
Weigh the client and compare with the admission weight
Collect a sputum specimen to rule out a new hospital-acquired pneumonia
optionRationales: Correct. Fluid volume excess is filling alveoli and blocking airflow; positioning upright and limiting more fluid address the cause right away.
Incorrect. Fine crackles from alveolar fluid do not clear with coughing; this targets rhonchi, not fluid volume excess.
Incorrect. Daily weight helps track fluid balance, but the client is already showing respiratory distress, so the nurse acts to stop the fluid first.
Incorrect. Testing for infection delays treatment of an obvious fluid-related cause of acute hypoxemia.
questions.rationale: Gas exchange requires inflated, well-oxygenated alveoli next to well-perfused capillaries. Fluid volume excess is one of the causes of blocked airflow into the alveolus: blood still flows past, but fluid instead of fresh air fills the sacs, so blood leaves the lungs poorly oxygenated. An older adult with heart failure receiving rapid fluids is at high risk. Sitting upright helps the lungs expand, and slowing the infusion stops the cause while the nurse notifies the provider; coughing is tempting, but crackles from fluid in the alveoli do not clear with a cough.
questions.takeaway: Fluid volume excess blocks airflow into the alveoli — stop adding fluid and position the client upright.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether the crackles come from secretions in large airways or fluid in the alveoli, and what caused the fluid.
questions.hintStrategy: When the nurse’s own intervention is causing harm, stopping or limiting it is usually the first action.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse reviews data for four assigned clients at the start of the shift. Refer to the exhibit. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: Client 1, admitted with COPD
Client 3, admitted with pneumonia
Client 4, recovering from hip arthroplasty
Client 2, admitted with an upper GI bleed
optionRationales: Incorrect. An SpO₂ of 89% is within this client’s prescribed target, and the client is speaking in full sentences.
Incorrect. Fever and a productive cough are expected with pneumonia, and the SpO₂ is acceptable on oxygen.
Incorrect. Mild postoperative anemia with controlled pain and ambulation is expected on day 3.
Correct. A hemoglobin of 6.2 g/dL with tachycardia and dizziness means oxygen delivery is failing even though the SpO₂ reads 99%.
questions.rationale: Oxygen delivery needs ventilated alveoli, perfused capillaries, and enough hemoglobin to carry oxygen. Client 2 has so little hemoglobin that, although every carrier is saturated (SpO₂ 99%), the tissues are not receiving enough oxygen — the heart is racing to compensate and the client is dizzy, and active bleeding may continue. The COPD client is tempting because 89% is the lowest number on the list, but it is within that client’s prescribed target. The nurse prioritizes the client whose data show unstable, worsening oxygen delivery.
questions.takeaway: The lowest SpO₂ is not always the sickest client — check whether there is enough hemoglobin to carry the oxygen.
questions.hintContent: Look beyond the SpO₂ column: which client has too few oxygen carriers and signs of compensation?
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each value with that client’s own expected range before calling it abnormal.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: During evening rounds, the nurse finds a client who is receiving continuous nasogastric tube feedings lying flat after a linen change. The client is coughing, RR is 28/min, and SpO₂ is 91% (95% an hour ago). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Auscultate the right lower lobe for new crackles
Stop the feeding and raise the head of the bed
Check tube placement by aspirating gastric contents
Notify the provider and request a chest x-ray
optionRationales: Incorrect. Auscultation is important, but aspiration may still be occurring, so it is stopped first.
Correct. Stopping the formula and positioning upright prevent further aspiration and help the lungs expand.
Incorrect. Placement is confirmed before the feeding is restarted, not while aspiration may be ongoing.
Incorrect. Notification follows the immediate actions that stop more formula from entering the lungs.
questions.rationale: Lying flat with formula running allows stomach contents to reflux and be aspirated. The right bronchus is shorter, wider, and straighter than the left, so aspirated material usually enters the right lung, often the right lower lobe. Because the client may still be aspirating, the first action is to remove the hazard — stop the feeding — and raise the head of the bed to protect the airway and improve chest expansion. Auscultating is tempting because “assess first” is a common rule, but when harm is actively occurring, the nurse stops the harm before collecting more data.
questions.takeaway: Suspected aspiration during a tube feeding: stop the feeding and sit the client up before anything else.
questions.hintContent: Think about whether the cause of the problem is still happening right now.
questions.hintStrategy: “Assess first” yields to “stop the harm” when an ongoing hazard is injuring the client.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 37-year-old client has bilateral nasal packing after septoplasty and must breathe through the mouth. On the second day the client reports a very dry, scratchy throat and thick secretions. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Mouth breathing skips the warming, moistening, and filtering your nose normally does.”
“The packing is pressing on your windpipe and narrowing the airway below it.”
“Your cilia are working harder to push the packing forward and out of your nose.”
“Mouth breathing lowers your blood oxygen level, and that is what dries the throat.”
optionRationales: Correct. The nares warm, humidify, and filter air; mouth breathing bypasses these functions, drying the airway and thickening secretions.
Incorrect. Nasal packing does not compress the trachea, and airway narrowing would not explain dryness.
Incorrect. Cilia sweep mucus and trapped particles; they do not push out packing, and this would not dry the throat.
Incorrect. Mouth breathing still delivers air to the alveoli; the dryness comes from lost humidification, not low oxygen.
questions.rationale: The nose is the primary entry point for air, and the nares and nasal passages warm, humidify, and filter it before it reaches the lower airway. When the nose is blocked, the client breathes through the mouth, which still moves air into the lungs but skips that conditioning. Dry, unconditioned air irritates the throat and thickens secretions. The tempting wrong answer links the dryness to low oxygen, but mouth breathing is a problem of air quality, not of how much oxygen reaches the blood.
questions.takeaway: Mouth breathing still ventilates the lungs but bypasses the nose’s warming, humidifying, and filtering.
questions.hintContent: Think about the jobs the nose performs on air that the mouth does not.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate explanations that name the wrong structure or the wrong mechanism, even if they sound clinical.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: On admission, a client with a hemoglobin of 6.6 g/dL had dyspnea walking to the bathroom, HR 120/min, and an SpO₂ of 98% on room air. Two units of packed red blood cells were transfused. Which finding best indicates that oxygen delivery to the tissues has improved?
options: SpO₂ is 99% on room air after the second unit is completed
PaO₂ is 96 mm Hg on the arterial blood gas drawn this morning
HR is 90/min, and the client walks to the bathroom without dyspnea
Respiratory rate is 18/min while the client is sleeping soundly
optionRationales: Incorrect. SpO₂ was already normal; it shows the percent of hemoglobin saturated, not how much oxygen is carried.
Incorrect. PaO₂ measures oxygen dissolved in plasma, which was never the problem, so it does not reflect carrying capacity.
Correct. A slower heart rate and better activity tolerance show the tissues now receive enough oxygen with less compensation.
Incorrect. A resting rate during sleep does not test whether oxygen delivery now meets demand during activity.
questions.rationale: Severe anemia limits oxygen delivery because there are too few hemoglobin “trucks,” even though each one is fully loaded — which is why the SpO₂ was 98% while the client was short of breath and tachycardic. The best evidence that a transfusion helped is a change in the very signs that showed the problem: the heart no longer has to race, and the client tolerates activity. SpO₂ and PaO₂ are tempting because they are oxygen numbers, but both were normal before treatment, so they cannot show improvement. Evaluate outcomes using the cues that were abnormal to begin with.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate an anemia intervention by compensation and activity tolerance, not by SpO₂.
questions.hintContent: Ask which of the client’s original findings were abnormal, then look for those to improve.
questions.hintStrategy: For “evaluate outcomes” items, pick the change in the cue that originally revealed the problem.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client using morphine patient-controlled analgesia after surgery is sleepy but arousable with a respiratory rate of 9/min. SpO₂ is 96% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. A nursing student says, “The saturation is fine, so the breathing must be okay.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “You’re right; the oxygen is doing its job, so we will keep watching the monitor.”
“Slow breathing lets carbon dioxide build up even when the saturation looks normal.”
“A slower rate is expected with opioids, so this number doesn’t concern me.”
“The saturation always drops first when a client isn’t breathing enough.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Agreeing reinforces unsafe reasoning; a rate below 10/min is bradypnea and must be acted on.
Correct. Supplemental oxygen can keep SpO₂ normal while hypoventilation causes CO₂ retention, so a rate of 9/min needs action.
Incorrect. Opioid effects on breathing are a risk to manage, not an expected finding to accept.
Incorrect. With supplemental oxygen, SpO₂ can stay normal long after CO₂ has started to climb.
questions.rationale: Oxygenation and ventilation are different jobs. Ventilation moves air in and out and removes CO₂; a pulse oximeter reports only how saturated hemoglobin is. A client breathing 9/min on supplemental oxygen can keep a normal SpO₂ while CO₂ accumulates, H⁺ rises, and respiratory acidosis develops. The tempting distractor claims SpO₂ will always fall first, but extra oxygen masks hypoventilation, so the nurse acts on the rate and sedation level instead of the saturation.
questions.takeaway: A normal SpO₂ on oxygen does not prove ventilation is adequate — watch the rate and sedation level.
questions.hintContent: Separate the two jobs: getting oxygen in versus getting carbon dioxide out.
questions.hintStrategy: In “best response to a colleague” items, choose the option that corrects unsafe reasoning with the correct principle.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 15-year-old with asthma asks the school nurse, “Why do the little tubes in my lungs squeeze shut during an attack when my windpipe never does?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Your windpipe is much wider, so mucus can’t block it the way it blocks the small tubes.”
“The small tubes have cartilage rings that swell up and close off during an attack.”
“Your windpipe has many more tiny hairs, and those hairs keep it from narrowing.”
“The small airways have muscle that can tighten; cartilage rings hold your windpipe open.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Width is not the reason; the small airways narrow mainly because their smooth muscle tightens.
Incorrect. This reverses the anatomy — bronchioles lack cartilage, which is why their muscle can narrow them.
Incorrect. Cilia sweep mucus out of the airways; they do not hold an airway open.
Correct. Bronchioles are supported by smooth muscle, which can spasm; the trachea and bronchi are held open by cartilage.
questions.rationale: The trachea and bronchi are supported by rings of cartilage, so they stay open. The bronchioles have no cartilage; they are supported by smooth muscle, which can tighten (bronchospasm) and narrow the airway — the core problem in an asthma attack. That is also why bronchodilators act on the bronchioles. The reversed-anatomy option is tempting because “cartilage” sounds technical, but cartilage is what prevents collapse, not what causes narrowing.
questions.takeaway: Cartilage keeps the trachea and bronchi open; smooth muscle lets the bronchioles narrow in bronchospasm.
questions.hintContent: Recall what supports the large airways versus the small ones.
questions.hintStrategy: For teaching items, choose the statement that is both accurate and pitched at the client’s level.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nursing student caring for a client with severe emphysema asks, “Her lungs are so full of air — why is her blood oxygen still low?” Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Thick sputum is blocking fresh air from ever getting into her damaged air sacs.”
“Her low carbon dioxide level has turned off the brain’s signal to breathe deeply.”
“Air reaches the damaged air sacs, but too little blood flows past to pick up oxygen.”
“Her hemoglobin has lost the ability to hold on to the oxygen molecules it carries.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sputum is an airflow problem; this client’s issue is the damaged alveolar–capillary bed.
Incorrect. Emphysema tends to raise CO₂, and a breathing-drive problem would not explain trapped air with low oxygen.
Correct. Emphysematous alveoli are a blood-flow (perfusion) problem: ventilation reaches the sacs, but perfusion past them is poor.
Incorrect. Emphysema damages the lung, not hemoglobin’s ability to bind oxygen.
questions.rationale: Gas exchange requires both inflated, well-oxygenated alveoli and well-perfused capillaries. In emphysema, overstretched, damaged alveoli lose much of the capillary network around them, so the air that sits in the lungs meets too little blood — a V/Q mismatch on the perfusion side. Blood leaving the lungs carries less oxygen even though the lungs feel “full.” Sputum blockage is tempting because COPD clients often have secretions, but sputum is an airflow problem and does not explain why air-filled lungs still fail to oxygenate blood.
questions.takeaway: Air in the alveoli helps only if enough blood flows past to pick up the oxygen.
questions.hintContent: Ask which half of the V/Q match is failing: air reaching the sacs, or blood reaching the air.
questions.hintStrategy: When options name different mechanisms, match the mechanism to the specific disease process.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 45-year-old client who smokes one pack of cigarettes a day asks why the cough is worst every morning and brings up so much mucus. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Smoke damages the tiny hairs that sweep mucus out, so it pools overnight until you cough.”
“Your lungs make mucus only while you sleep, so the morning is the only time it can come out.”
“Lying flat squeezes the cartilage in your windpipe, which traps mucus until you sit up.”
“Nicotine relaxes the muscle in your small airways, which pulls mucus down into them.”
optionRationales: Correct. Cilia normally sweep mucus upward; smoke impairs them, so secretions pool during sleep and are cleared by coughing in the morning.
Incorrect. Mucus is produced continuously; the morning cough reflects pooled secretions, not night-only production.
Incorrect. Cartilage holds the trachea open in every position; it does not trap mucus.
Incorrect. Smooth muscle relaxation does not pull mucus into airways; the issue is impaired clearance by cilia.
questions.rationale: Cilia are tiny hair-like projections that beat in waves to move mucus and trapped particles up and out of the airways, where they are coughed out or swallowed. Cigarette smoke impairs this protective mechanism, so mucus stays in the airways, pools during the night, and is coughed up on waking. Explaining the mechanism in plain words supports the client’s understanding of why quitting helps. The night-only production option is tempting because it matches the timing, but it gets the physiology wrong.
questions.takeaway: Smoking impairs ciliary clearance, so mucus pools overnight and the morning cough clears it.
questions.hintContent: Think about which airway defense normally moves mucus out without the client noticing.
questions.hintStrategy: Prefer the option that names the correct protective structure and its job.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: Thirty minutes after a subclavian central venous catheter was inserted, a client develops sudden dyspnea, absent breath sounds on the right, and decreased right chest rise. After applying oxygen and notifying the provider, the nurse hears the client ask, “How could my lung collapse from an IV line?” Which explanation is accurate?
options: “The catheter may have slipped into the main airway that leads to your right lung.”
“IV fluid may have flowed into the air sacs of your right lung and filled them up.”
“The needle may have torn the cartilage rings that normally hold your lung open.”
“Air may have entered the space around your lung and removed the suction holding it open.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A venous catheter is not placed in the airway; collapse here results from air in the pleural space.
Incorrect. Fluid-filled alveoli cause crackles, not absent breath sounds with decreased chest rise.
Incorrect. Cartilage supports the trachea and bronchi, not the lung; lung expansion depends on pleural pressure.
Correct. Negative pressure in the pleural space holds the lung against the chest wall; air in that space removes it, and the lung collapses.
questions.rationale: Each lung is wrapped in two pleural layers — the visceral pleura on the lung and the parietal pleura on the chest wall — with the pleural space between them. Pressure in that space is normally negative, and that slight suction keeps the lung stretched out against the chest wall. A needle passing near the lung apex during subclavian insertion can let air into the pleural space (pneumothorax), the negative pressure is lost, and the lung collapses — causing absent breath sounds and decreased chest rise on that side. The torn-cartilage option is tempting but confuses airway support with lung expansion.
questions.takeaway: Air in the pleural space eliminates the negative pressure that keeps the lung expanded.
questions.hintContent: Recall what normally holds the lung against the chest wall.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the explanation to all the findings: absent sounds plus decreased chest rise means air, not fluid.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nurse is caring for several clients with hypoxemia. Which clients’ hypoxemia results mainly from blocked airflow into the alveoli? Select all that apply.
options: A client with thick sputum plugging the bronchi during pneumonia
A client with swollen, inflamed airways from acute bronchitis
A client with emphysema and overstretched, damaged alveoli
A client with fluid volume excess and crackles throughout both lungs
A client with collapsed alveoli at both bases after abdominal surgery
A client with a clot lodged in a branch of the pulmonary artery
optionRationales: Correct. Sputum blocks air from reaching the alveoli, a ventilation-side V/Q problem.
Correct. Inflammation narrows the airway and limits air reaching the alveoli.
Incorrect. Emphysematous alveoli are listed on the blood-flow side: air arrives, but little blood comes by.
Correct. Fluid filling the alveoli prevents fresh air from reaching the blood.
Correct. Atelectasis keeps air out of the alveoli while blood still flows past.
Incorrect. A clot blocks blood flow through the capillaries — a perfusion problem, not an airflow problem.
questions.rationale: Every V/Q mismatch is either “air can’t get to the blood” or “blood can’t get to the air.” Airflow into the alveolus is blocked by sputum, inflammation, atelectasis, and fluid volume excess; blood flow through the capillary is blocked by clots, plaque buildup, and emphysematous alveoli. Emphysema is the most tempting wrong choice because it is a lung disease with air trapping, but in this framework the damaged alveoli are poorly perfused rather than poorly ventilated. Sorting the cause tells the nurse which interventions will help — airway clearance and lung expansion for airflow problems.
questions.takeaway: Sputum, inflammation, atelectasis, and fluid block airflow; clots, plaque, and emphysematous alveoli block blood flow.
questions.hintContent: For each client, ask whether air or blood is failing to reach the alveolar–capillary meeting point.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each SATA option independently against one rule rather than comparing options.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: During a wellness visit, a nurse observes the breathing of a healthy 34-year-old client at rest. Which findings are expected? Select all that apply.
options: The respiratory rate is 16 breaths/min
The chest rises and falls equally on both sides
Exhalation lasts about twice as long as inhalation
Inhalation lasts noticeably longer than exhalation
Neck muscles stay relaxed during quiet breathing
The sternocleidomastoid muscles tighten with each breath
optionRationales: Correct. A rate of 16/min is within the adult range of 12–20/min.
Correct. Symmetric chest movement is expected in healthy lungs.
Correct. Inspiration normally takes about half as long as expiration.
Incorrect. This reverses the normal timing of a resting breath.
Correct. At rest, breathing is effortless and does not recruit accessory neck muscles.
Incorrect. Visible neck-muscle contraction signals increased work of breathing, not normal breathing.
questions.rationale: Normal, effortless breathing (eupnea) has a rate within the age-expected range, relaxed neck muscles, and symmetric chest rise and fall. Inspiration is quick and expiration is slower and more relaxed, taking about twice as long. Recognizing the normal pattern is what lets the nurse spot an abnormal one quickly. The timing option is the most commonly missed, because students often assume breathing in and out take equal time.
questions.takeaway: Normal adult breathing: 12–20/min, relaxed neck muscles, symmetric chest, and exhalation about twice as long as inhalation.
questions.hintContent: Picture a calm person breathing quietly — which muscles move, and which phase takes longer?
questions.hintStrategy: In “expected findings” items, eliminate any option that signals extra effort.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with pneumonia has a PaO₂ of 62 mm Hg and an SaO₂ of 90%. Which findings indicate that the low blood oxygen is now affecting oxygen delivery to the tissues? Select all that apply.
options: Fatigue after brushing teeth at the sink
Yellow sputum with a productive cough
New difficulty following simple directions
PaO₂ of 62 mm Hg on the arterial blood gas
Increasing irritability with staff and family
SaO₂ of 90% on the arterial blood gas
optionRationales: Correct. Fatigue with minimal activity reflects tissues not receiving enough oxygen.
Incorrect. Purulent sputum reflects the infection, not the effect of low oxygen on tissues.
Correct. The brain is very sensitive to low oxygen; new confusion shows tissue hypoxia.
Incorrect. A low PaO₂ defines hypoxemia (blood level), not tissue hypoxia.
Correct. Irritability is an early sign that the tissues, especially the brain, are underoxygenated.
Incorrect. A low SaO₂ is also a blood measure of hypoxemia, not evidence of tissue effects.
questions.rationale: Hypoxemia is a low oxygen level in the blood; hypoxia is decreased oxygen delivery to the tissues, and untreated hypoxemia leads to hypoxia. The blood-gas values document hypoxemia but say nothing on their own about the tissues. Tissue effects show up in the client: mild impairments cause fatigue, irritability, and discomfort, and the oxygen-hungry brain produces confusion. The PaO₂ and SaO₂ options tempt students because they are oxygen values, but they are measurements of the blood, not of the tissues.
questions.takeaway: Hypoxemia is measured in the blood; hypoxia shows up in the client’s brain, energy, and behavior.
questions.hintContent: Separate findings measured in the blood sample from findings you observe in the client.
questions.hintStrategy: When two terms look alike, define each one first, then sort the options by definition.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client has postoperative atelectasis and a newly diagnosed deep vein thrombosis in the left calf. The nurse reviews the plan of care. Which interventions target the airflow (ventilation) side of the client’s V/Q problem? Select all that apply.
options: Anticoagulant therapy as prescribed
Monitoring for sudden dyspnea with clear breath sounds
Sitting upright in a chair for meals
Incentive spirometry 10 times every hour while awake
Coughing and deep-breathing exercises every 2 hours
optionRationales: Incorrect. Anticoagulation addresses the clot and blood flow — the perfusion side.
Incorrect. This surveils for a clot reaching the lungs, a perfusion problem.
Correct. Upright positioning lowers the diaphragm and helps the lungs expand.
Correct. Slow, deep breaths reexpand collapsed alveoli so air can reach them again.
Correct. These clear secretions and open alveoli, improving airflow.
questions.rationale: Atelectasis is a ventilation problem: collapsed alveoli receive no fresh air even though blood flows past them. Interventions that target airflow open and inflate alveoli — incentive spirometry, coughing and deep breathing, and upright positioning. The deep vein thrombosis creates a different risk: a clot reaching the lung would block blood flow (perfusion). Anticoagulation is tempting because it is important for this client, but it does nothing to reinflate collapsed alveoli.
questions.takeaway: Lung-expansion measures treat airflow problems; anticoagulation addresses blood-flow problems.
questions.hintContent: For each intervention, ask whether it changes air reaching the alveoli or blood reaching them.
questions.hintStrategy: A correct intervention can still be the wrong answer if it does not match the specific goal in the stem.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A healthy 40-year-old runs up three flights of stairs, and carbon dioxide production in the muscles increases. Which changes would the nurse expect as the body responds? Select all that apply.
options: Arterial pH rises above 7.45
Breaths become deeper
The respiratory rate increases
The hydrogen ion (H⁺) concentration in arterial blood rises
Breathing slows to conserve oxygen for the muscles
optionRationales: Incorrect. More H⁺ makes the blood more acidic, so pH falls rather than rises.
Correct. The drive to breathe increases depth as well as rate to blow off CO₂.
Correct. Rising H⁺ stimulates the brain to speed up breathing.
Correct. CO₂ combines with water to form acid, so rising CO₂ raises H⁺.
Incorrect. Rising CO₂ speeds breathing; slowing would let CO₂ climb further.
questions.rationale: The respiratory drive is stimulated primarily by the concentration of H⁺ in arterial blood, which changes directly with CO₂. During exercise CO₂ rises, H⁺ rises, and pH drifts down; the brain responds by increasing the rate and depth of breathing to blow off CO₂ and return pH toward normal. The reverse happens when CO₂ falls. The pH option tempts students who remember “CO₂ changes pH” but forget the direction: more CO₂ means more acid and a lower pH.
questions.takeaway: Rising CO₂ → more H⁺ → lower pH → faster, deeper breathing.
questions.hintContent: Follow the chain: CO₂ to H⁺ to pH to the brain’s signal to breathe.
questions.hintStrategy: For cause-and-effect chains, check the direction of every arrow before selecting.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A nurse in a family practice clinic reviews the respiratory rates recorded for clients seen this morning. Which rates require follow-up because they are outside the expected range for the client’s age? Select all that apply.
options: Newborn, 48 breaths/min
School-age child, 20 breaths/min
Older adult, 17 breaths/min
Adolescent, 26 breaths/min
Toddler, 28 breaths/min
Preschooler, 42 breaths/min
optionRationales: Incorrect. Within the 30–60/min expected for newborns.
Incorrect. Within the 16–22/min expected for school-age children.
Incorrect. Within the 15–20/min expected for older adults.
Correct. Above the 12–20/min expected for adolescents (tachypnea).
Incorrect. Within the 20–40/min expected for toddlers.
Correct. Above the 20–35/min expected for preschoolers.
questions.rationale: A respiratory rate means little until it is compared with the expected range for the client’s age. Rates fall steadily with age: newborns and infants 30–60/min, toddlers 20–40, preschoolers 20–35, school-age children 16–22, and adolescents and adults 12–20, with older adults at 15–20. A preschooler at 42 and an adolescent at 26 are both above range and need reassessment. The newborn’s 48 is the most tempting wrong pick because it would be alarming in an adult, but it is normal for a newborn.
questions.takeaway: Always interpret a respiratory rate against the age-specific normal range.
questions.hintContent: Picture the age-range table and slide each client into the correct row.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each SATA option on its own against a standard, not against the other options.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client 4 days after hip arthroplasty develops sudden dyspnea and an SpO₂ of 88% on room air. Which findings support a blood-flow (perfusion) problem rather than an airflow problem as the cause? Select all that apply.
options: Equal chest expansion on both sides
Diminished breath sounds at the bases with shallow breathing
Clear breath sounds in all lobes
Fine crackles at both bases that do not clear with coughing
Thick yellow sputum with a frequent cough
Swelling and tenderness of the operative-side calf
optionRationales: Correct. Symmetric expansion argues against collapse or blockage of airflow.
Incorrect. This suggests atelectasis, which blocks airflow into the alveoli.
Correct. Clear lungs mean air is reaching the alveoli, pointing to a blood-flow problem.
Incorrect. Crackles indicate fluid or collapsed alveoli, an airflow problem.
Incorrect. Secretions block airways, an airflow problem.
Correct. A probable deep vein thrombosis is a source of a clot that can block pulmonary blood flow.
questions.rationale: When a client suddenly becomes hypoxemic, the lung examination helps sort the cause. Clear breath sounds and symmetric expansion show air is moving into the alveoli, so the likely failure is on the perfusion side — a clot blocking blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries — and a swollen, tender calf after hip surgery suggests where the clot came from. Crackles, diminished bases, and thick sputum all point to airflow problems such as atelectasis, fluid, or secretions. The diminished-bases option is tempting because atelectasis is common after surgery, but it would indicate the airflow side.
questions.takeaway: Sudden hypoxemia with clear, symmetric lungs and a risk factor for clots points to blocked blood flow.
questions.hintContent: Abnormal breath sounds mean air is having trouble; normal breath sounds shift suspicion to the blood side.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each cue into one of two buckets before selecting — here, airflow versus blood flow.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: In the emergency department, a 33-year-old client with asthma was wheezing loudly throughout both lungs an hour ago. Now the nurse hears almost no air movement in any lung field. The client is drowsy, slumped in bed, and answers with one word. SpO₂ is 88% on oxygen. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Increase the oxygen flow and recheck the SpO₂
Call the rapid response team for immediate help
Obtain a peak flow reading to grade the attack
Request a stat arterial blood gas to check CO₂
optionRationales: Incorrect. More oxygen may help briefly, but it does not move air through closed airways or support a tiring client, who needs a team now.
Correct. Diminished sounds after loud wheezing with drowsiness means airflow is failing and the client is tiring — an emergency requiring escalation.
Incorrect. Peak flow measures severity, but a drowsy client giving one-word answers cannot perform it, and testing delays rescue.
Incorrect. An ABG will likely show rising CO₂, but the clinical picture already shows failing ventilation, and waiting for results delays help.
questions.rationale: Wheezing requires air moving through narrowed airways. When a wheezing client suddenly becomes quiet on auscultation, the airways may be so narrowed — or the client so exhausted — that almost no air is moving (a “silent chest”). Combined with drowsiness, one-word answers, and a falling SpO₂, this is a life-threatening deterioration that requires immediate escalation. Turning up the oxygen or ordering more tests is the tempting trap: they feel like action, but this client is tiring toward respiratory arrest and needs a rapid response team now.
questions.takeaway: A wheezing client whose chest goes quiet and who becomes drowsy is deteriorating, not improving.
questions.hintContent: Ask what must be happening for a wheeze to be heard, then ask why it might disappear.
questions.hintStrategy: When a sign “improves” while the client looks worse, believe the client and escalate.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: Forty minutes after extubation, a client in the intensive care unit develops a loud, high-pitched crowing sound on inspiration that the nurse can hear from the doorway. The client is anxious and grasping the side rails. SpO₂ is 92% on a face mask. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Stay with the client and call for emergency help
Ask the client to cough, then listen again for clearing
Recheck the SpO₂ and count the respiratory rate
Give the client’s PRN albuterol inhaler from the bedside
optionRationales: Correct. Inspiratory stridor signals upper airway narrowing that can close completely; the nurse stays and summons help to secure the airway.
Incorrect. Coughing clears rhonchi, not stridor; this delays action for an airway emergency.
Incorrect. Vital signs help track the trend, but audible stridor already signals upper airway narrowing, and gathering numbers delays getting help.
Incorrect. An inhaler targets lower-airway bronchospasm and cannot be used effectively by a client in upper-airway distress.
questions.rationale: Stridor is a loud, high-pitched crowing sound on inspiration, often audible without a stethoscope, caused by narrowing of the upper airway — after extubation, usually from laryngeal edema. Because the airway can close completely, stridor is an emergency: the nurse stays with the client, calls for help, and prepares to support the airway. Asking the client to cough is the tempting choice because it is the right move for rhonchi, but stridor does not clear with coughing and time spent “re-listening” is time lost.
questions.takeaway: Stridor after extubation is an airway emergency — stay with the client and call for help.
questions.hintContent: Identify where in the airway a sound heard on inspiration from the doorway is coming from.
questions.hintStrategy: Airway threats come first; eliminate any option that delays action to gather more data.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A nurse is caring for four clients with hypoxemia on a pulmonary unit. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client whose HR has risen from 84 to 110/min, who is restless and picking at the sheets
A client with COPD who has clubbed fingers and an SpO₂ of 90% on 2 L/min
A client whose HR has dropped from 118 to 52/min, with BP 82/50 mm Hg and lethargy
A client with pneumonia who reports sharp pain on deep breaths in one spot
optionRationales: Incorrect. Tachycardia and restlessness are early, compensated signs; urgent, but less critical than decompensation.
Incorrect. Clubbing reflects long-standing hypoxemia, and the SpO₂ is likely within this client’s target.
Correct. Bradycardia, hypotension, and decreasing alertness are late signs of hypoxia — compensation is failing.
Incorrect. Pleuritic pain needs attention, but it does not signal the immediate collapse seen in late hypoxia.
questions.rationale: Early hypoxia shows the body compensating: restlessness, anxiety, tachycardia, tachypnea, and often a higher blood pressure. Late hypoxia shows compensation failing: bradycardia, hypotension, central cyanosis, and stupor. A heart rate that falls from 118 to 52 in a hypoxic client means the heart itself is running out of oxygen, so this client is closest to arrest. The restless, tachycardic client is the tempting choice because the signs are dramatic and new, but those are early signs that still allow a brief window for intervention.
questions.takeaway: Bradycardia and hypotension in a hypoxic client mean decompensation — see that client first.
questions.hintContent: Separate signs of the body compensating from signs of compensation failing.
questions.hintStrategy: Rank by how close each client is to arrest: late signs outrank early signs.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 58-year-old client is 1 day postoperative after an open gastrectomy. The client has become restless and keeps trying to sit up. Refer to the exhibit. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the PRN antihypertensive for the elevated blood pressure
Raise the head of the bed and check the SpO₂ and breath sounds
Give the PRN opioid because restlessness suggests uncontrolled pain
Recheck the vital signs in 1 hour to look for a trend
optionRationales: Incorrect. The BP rise is part of the compensatory response to hypoxia; lowering it treats a number, not the cause.
Correct. Rising HR, RR, and BP with restlessness are early signs of hypoxia, so the nurse positions the client and assesses oxygenation.
Incorrect. An opioid may depress breathing before hypoxia has been ruled out.
Incorrect. The trend is already clear over the past hour; waiting allows hypoxia to progress to late signs.
questions.rationale: Early hypoxia is the body compensating: the brain signals with restlessness, the heart speeds up, breathing quickens, and blood pressure often rises. Late hypoxia brings bradycardia, hypotension, and cyanosis. This client shows the early pattern, so the nurse acts now — raises the head of the bed and assesses SpO₂ and breath sounds — while there is still time to reverse the cause, such as postoperative atelectasis. The antihypertensive is tempting because the BP is high, but treating it hides one of the compensating signs and misses the real problem.
questions.takeaway: Early hypoxia raises HR, RR, and often BP — treat the oxygenation problem, not the individual numbers.
questions.hintContent: Look at the three vital signs together rather than one at a time.
questions.hintStrategy: When several abnormal findings share one cause, choose the option that addresses the cause.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 30-year-old client with asthma walks into an urgent care clinic and sits on the edge of the exam table leaning forward with hands on the knees. The client speaks two words at a time in a hoarse voice. RR is 32/min and SpO₂ is 94% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Obtain a detailed history of the client’s asthma triggers and inhaler use
Auscultate all lung fields carefully before starting any treatment
Obtain a peak expiratory flow reading to grade the attack’s severity
Keep the client upright, apply oxygen as prescribed, and get the provider
optionRationales: Incorrect. The history matters, but a client in severe distress needs immediate support before an interview.
Incorrect. Lung sounds are part of the assessment, but tripod posture and two-word speech already show severe distress, so treatment should not wait.
Incorrect. Peak flow helps grade asthma severity, but a client speaking two words at a time needs oxygen and the provider first.
Correct. Tripod positioning and two-word speech mean severe distress regardless of the SpO₂, so the nurse supports breathing and gets help.
questions.rationale: Posture and speech are powerful assessment clues. The tripod position helps the chest expand and signals significant respiratory distress, and a client who can speak only one to three words per breath is in severe distress no matter what the pulse oximeter shows. A hoarse voice and RR of 32 add to the picture. The nurse keeps the client upright, applies oxygen as prescribed, and gets the provider. The tempting trap is the 94% SpO₂, which can make the situation look mild; treat the client, not the number.
questions.takeaway: Tripod posture and speaking only a few words mean severe distress, whatever the SpO₂.
questions.hintContent: Look at what the client’s posture and speech are telling you before you look at the monitor.
questions.hintStrategy: When the client’s appearance and a device reading conflict, act on the client’s appearance.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A farmworker is admitted after a fall onto a fence post that injured the right chest. On palpation the nurse feels a crackling, “crispy rice” sensation under the skin of the right chest that now extends to the base of the neck, and the client’s voice is becoming hoarse. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Mark the edges of the crepitus to track how far it spreads
Document crepitus as an expected finding after chest trauma
Assess the airway and notify the provider of the spreading crepitus
Raise the head of the bed and recheck the area in 1 hour
optionRationales: Incorrect. Marking the border is a useful way to track spread, but the crepitus already reaches the neck with hoarseness, so the airway comes first.
Incorrect. Crepitus is never expected; its source must be found, especially when it is spreading.
Correct. Crepitus means air is trapped in the tissues; spreading toward the neck with voice change threatens the airway.
Incorrect. Raising the head of the bed can ease breathing, but waiting an hour to recheck delays reporting a possible airway threat.
questions.rationale: Crepitus is a crackling feeling under the skin caused by air trapped in the tissues, seen after chest trauma, around chest tubes, or with an air leak. It is not an expected finding, and its source must be identified. Air spreading toward the neck can compress structures around the airway, and a new hoarse voice is a warning sign of airway involvement. The nurse assesses the airway and notifies the provider promptly. Documenting it as expected is tempting because it often follows chest injury, but “common after trauma” is not the same as “normal.”
questions.takeaway: Crepitus is air in the tissues — find the source, and treat spreading crepitus with voice change as an airway threat.
questions.hintContent: Ask where the air under the skin is coming from and what it could press on as it spreads.
questions.hintStrategy: Any finding that progresses toward the airway moves to the top of the priority list.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: An AP reports data collected on four clients. Refer to the exhibit. Which client should the RN assess first?

rows: SpO₂ 89% on 2 L/min (target 88–92%); talking with visitors
Temp 38.1°C (100.6°F); RR 22/min; coughing up yellow sputum
“Her voice sounds hoarse, and her breathing got noisy when she breathes in.”
Used rescue inhaler 30 minutes ago; now resting, RR 18/min, SpO₂ 96%

options: Client C, who had a thyroidectomy 6 hours ago
Client A, who has COPD and is talking with visitors
Client B, who has pneumonia and a low-grade fever
Client D, who has asthma and used a rescue inhaler
optionRationales: Correct. New hoarseness with noisy inspiration after neck surgery suggests stridor from upper airway swelling — an emergency.
Incorrect. An SpO₂ of 89% is within this client’s prescribed target, and the client is talking comfortably.
Incorrect. Mild fever and productive cough are expected on day 2 of treatment for pneumonia.
Incorrect. The client responded to the rescue inhaler and now has normal vital signs.
questions.rationale: An AP can measure and report data, but the RN interprets it. “Noisy breathing when she breathes in” in a client 6 hours after neck surgery describes possible stridor — a high-pitched inspiratory sound from upper airway narrowing, such as swelling around the larynx — and the new hoarse voice supports it. Upper airway obstruction can progress to complete closure, so this client is seen first. Client A is tempting because an 89% SpO₂ looks low, but it is within the prescribed target, and the client is talking comfortably.
questions.takeaway: New noisy inspiration with hoarseness after neck surgery is possible stridor — assess immediately.
questions.hintContent: Translate the AP’s plain-language description into an assessment term, then judge its urgency.
questions.hintStrategy: Airway problems outrank breathing and circulation findings, and expected findings rank last.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: During an admission interview, a 42-year-old client with asthma reports several findings. Which finding requires the nurse’s priority follow-up?
options: Smoking 10 pack-years in the past but quitting 15 years ago
Having seasonal allergies that flare up every spring
Waking up at night coughing about once a month lately
Using the rescue inhaler four times a day for the past week
optionRationales: Incorrect. A remote smoking history is a risk factor to document, not an active problem.
Incorrect. Allergies are a known trigger to note, but they are a stable, expected part of the history.
Incorrect. Night symptoms are worth noting, but waking twice a month or less still fits well-controlled asthma, unlike daily rescue-inhaler use.
Correct. Frequent rescue-inhaler use means the asthma is poorly controlled and may be heading toward a serious exacerbation.
questions.rationale: The medication history should include how often the client uses the rescue inhaler, because frequency is a direct measure of asthma control. Needing a rescue inhaler four times a day signals that the airways are repeatedly narrowing and that the client may be heading toward a severe attack — a warning sign that needs prompt follow-up with the provider. A remote smoking history is tempting because smoking is a major respiratory risk factor, but it is past and stable. Current, worsening data outrank historical risk factors.
questions.takeaway: Frequent rescue-inhaler use is a red flag for poorly controlled asthma.
questions.hintContent: Ask which history item describes what is happening now and getting worse.
questions.hintStrategy: In history items, current and worsening problems outrank past or stable risk factors.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A family member of an 84-year-old resident in a long-term care facility tells the nurse, “Mom is confused today, but she gets senile when she’s tired.” The resident was oriented yesterday. RR is 26/min, HR 108/min, and temperature 37.9°C (100.2°F). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Reorient the resident and limit visitors so she can rest
Check the SpO₂ and auscultate the lungs
Ask the family to describe her usual level of orientation
Obtain a urine specimen to check for an infection
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reorientation treats the behavior but ignores a possible physiologic cause.
Correct. New confusion with tachypnea and tachycardia is a possible sign of hypoxia, so the nurse assesses oxygenation first.
Incorrect. Baseline history matters, but the nurse already knows she was oriented yesterday, and abnormal vital signs need assessment first.
Incorrect. Urinary infection often causes confusion in older adults, but the fast breathing points to oxygenation, which is assessed first.
questions.rationale: Unexplained, sudden confusion is one of the classic signs of hypoxia because the brain uses a large amount of oxygen and has almost no reserve. In an older adult — who has a weaker cough reflex and a higher risk of infection and aspiration — new confusion with tachypnea, tachycardia, and a low-grade fever suggests a developing respiratory problem such as pneumonia. The nurse checks SpO₂ and listens to the lungs before accepting any other explanation. A urinary infection is tempting because it often causes confusion in older adults, but the rapid breathing points to oxygenation first, and she was oriented yesterday, so this is new.
questions.takeaway: Sudden confusion in an older adult is a hypoxia cue until oxygenation has been assessed.
questions.hintContent: Compare today’s mental status with yesterday’s, then look at the respiratory rate.
questions.hintStrategy: Rule out physiologic causes before accepting a behavioral or chronic explanation for a new change.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 50-year-old Black client is dyspneic and restless, and the nurse suspects central cyanosis. Where should the nurse inspect to best detect it?
options: The oral mucosa and the conjunctivae
The skin of the forearms and the back of the hands
The fingertips under the pulse oximeter probe
The soles of the feet and the toes
optionRationales: Correct. Cyanosis can be hard to see in darker skin, so the nurse inspects the lips, tongue, oral mucosa, and conjunctivae.
Incorrect. Skin pigmentation can hide color change, so these sites are unreliable for central cyanosis.
Incorrect. Fingertips show peripheral, not central, cyanosis and can be affected by cold or poor circulation.
Incorrect. These are peripheral sites that reflect local circulation, not central oxygenation.
questions.rationale: Cyanosis is a late sign of hypoxia, and it can be difficult to see in darker skin. Central cyanosis — in the lips, tongue, and mucous membranes — is more serious than peripheral cyanosis, so the nurse looks where pigment is least likely to mask color change: the oral mucosa and conjunctivae. Peripheral sites such as fingertips and toes are tempting because they are where cyanosis is often taught, but they reflect local circulation and miss central color change. Because cyanosis appears late, the nurse also relies on early signs such as restlessness and tachycardia.
questions.takeaway: In darker skin, assess the oral mucosa and conjunctivae for cyanosis — and don’t wait for it.
questions.hintContent: Think about where pigment is least likely to hide a color change.
questions.hintStrategy: For skin-color items, choose the site that is accurate for every client, not only for lighter skin.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: An older adult is admitted with left lower lobe pneumonia confirmed by chest x-ray. Which assessment finding over the left lower lobe would the nurse consider unexpected?
options: Dullness on percussion
Fine crackles that do not clear with coughing
Decreased tactile fremitus
Loud, high-pitched bronchial breath sounds
optionRationales: Incorrect. Solid, fluid-filled lung tissue sounds dull rather than resonant.
Incorrect. Fluid in the alveoli produces crackles that usually persist after a cough.
Correct. Consolidated lung carries vibration well, so fremitus should be increased, not decreased.
Incorrect. Consolidation carries tracheal-type sounds to the surface, an expected change.
questions.rationale: Consolidation means the alveoli are filled with fluid or pus and the lung has become solid. Sound and vibration travel better through solids and fluid than through air, so over consolidated lung the nurse expects increased tactile fremitus, dullness on percussion, bronchial breath sounds in a peripheral field, and crackles. Decreased fremitus would point instead to extra air or a barrier, such as a pneumothorax or air trapping. Bronchial sounds tempt students to call them unexpected because they are abnormal at the bases, but in consolidation they are exactly what the nurse expects.
questions.takeaway: Consolidation increases fremitus; air (pneumothorax or trapping) decreases it.
questions.hintContent: Remember whether vibration travels better through solid tissue or through air.
questions.hintStrategy: For “unexpected finding” items, find the option that contradicts the diagnosis.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: While auscultating a healthy adult client, the nurse hears medium-pitched breath sounds between the scapulae with inspiration and expiration of equal length. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: Bronchial sounds suggesting underlying consolidation
Normal bronchovesicular sounds in their expected location
Vesicular sounds that are louder than expected at this site
Diminished sounds indicating early air trapping
optionRationales: Incorrect. Bronchial sounds are loud and high-pitched with a longer expiration; these sounds are medium-pitched with equal phases.
Correct. Bronchovesicular sounds are normal beside the sternum and between the scapulae, with equal inspiration and expiration.
Incorrect. Vesicular sounds are soft, low-pitched, and longer on inspiration, and are heard over the periphery.
Incorrect. Medium-pitched sounds with equal phases are not diminished; they are a normal pattern.
questions.rationale: Each of the three normal breath sounds has a characteristic pitch, timing, and location. Bronchial sounds are loud and high-pitched over the trachea with a longer expiration; bronchovesicular sounds are medium in pitch and loudness with equal phases beside the sternum and between the scapulae; vesicular sounds are soft and low-pitched with a longer inspiration over the peripheral fields and bases. A normal sound is abnormal only when heard in the wrong place. Students who memorize “bronchial = consolidation” may overcall these sounds, but this sound is in its expected location.
questions.takeaway: Right sound, right place is normal: bronchovesicular sounds belong between the scapulae and beside the sternum.
questions.hintContent: Match the pitch, the timing, and the location to one normal breath sound.
questions.hintStrategy: Before labeling a sound abnormal, check whether it belongs where you heard it.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: While auscultating a client with heart failure, the nurse hears brief, high-pitched popping sounds at both lung bases late in inspiration that are unchanged after the client coughs. How should the nurse document this finding?
options: Rhonchi at both bases from secretions in the large airways
Expiratory wheezes at both bases from narrowed small airways
A pleural friction rub at both bases from inflamed pleural layers
Fine crackles at both bases, consistent with fluid in the alveoli
optionRationales: Incorrect. Rhonchi are low-pitched and snoring, and they often clear or change with coughing.
Incorrect. Wheezes are continuous, musical, high-pitched sounds, usually on expiration — not brief pops.
Incorrect. A friction rub is a grating, leathery sound in a localized spot on both inspiration and expiration.
Correct. Brief, high-pitched popping late in inspiration that persists after coughing describes fine crackles from alveolar fluid.
questions.rationale: Fine crackles are brief, high-pitched popping sounds, usually late in inspiration, caused by fluid in the alveoli or collapsed alveoli popping open — common in pneumonia, atelectasis, and fluid volume excess such as heart failure. They usually do not clear with coughing. Rhonchi are the most tempting wrong answer because both are “wet” sounds, but rhonchi are low-pitched, snoring or gurgling sounds from secretions in larger airways and often clear after a cough. Asking the client to cough and re-listening is how the nurse tells them apart.
questions.takeaway: Crackles that persist after a cough mean fluid in the alveoli; rhonchi often clear with coughing.
questions.hintContent: Use pitch, timing, and the response to coughing to identify the sound.
questions.hintStrategy: When two sounds seem alike, find the single feature that separates them and look for it in the stem.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 54-year-old client reports smoking 1½ packs of cigarettes per day since age 34. How many pack-years should the nurse document?
options: 20 pack-years
51 pack-years
30 pack-years
81 pack-years
optionRationales: Incorrect. This counts only the years smoked and ignores the 1.5 packs per day.
Incorrect. This multiplies packs per day by the age the client started smoking (34) instead of by the years smoked.
Correct. 1.5 packs/day × 20 years of smoking = 30 pack-years.
Incorrect. This multiplies packs per day by the client’s age instead of by the years smoked.
questions.rationale: Pack-years quantify lifetime smoking exposure: packs smoked per day multiplied by the number of years smoked. The client started at 34 and is now 54, so the client has smoked for 20 years; 1.5 × 20 = 30 pack-years. The most common error is using the client’s age rather than the years smoked, which greatly inflates the number. Accurate pack-years help the provider judge risk for COPD and lung cancer and guide screening.
questions.takeaway: Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked (not the client’s age).
questions.hintContent: First calculate how many years the client has actually smoked.
questions.hintStrategy: For calculation items, identify each quantity the formula needs before multiplying.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: During a home visit, a client with heart failure reports waking at night short of breath. Which question should the nurse ask to best track the severity of the client’s orthopnea over time?
options: “How many pillows do you need to sleep comfortably?”
“Do you get short of breath climbing a flight of stairs?”
“How often do you wake up suddenly at night gasping for air?”
“Is your cough worse in the morning or at night?”
optionRationales: Correct. Orthopnea is breathlessness when lying flat; the number of pillows needed gives a simple, measurable way to track change over time.
Incorrect. This is a useful heart failure question, but it measures dyspnea on exertion, not breathlessness when lying flat.
Incorrect. Asking about sudden night waking is reasonable in heart failure, but it measures paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, not how flat the client can lie.
Incorrect. Cough timing can reflect fluid or airway problems, but it does not quantify the client’s ability to lie flat.
questions.rationale: Orthopnea is difficulty breathing when lying flat, relieved by sitting up. Because the client props up to breathe, the number of pillows needed to sleep — or the need to sleep in a recliner — gives the nurse a simple, measurable way to track whether the condition is improving or worsening. Documenting “orthopnea, 3 pillows” lets the next nurse compare. The exertion question is tempting because it also measures breathlessness, but it assesses activity tolerance rather than breathing when supine.
questions.takeaway: Track orthopnea by the number of pillows the client needs to sleep.
questions.hintContent: Define orthopnea, then pick the question that measures it.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the question that yields measurable data about the specific symptom named in the stem.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A nurse observes a nursing student auscultating a client’s lungs. Which action by the student requires correction?
options: Comparing one side of the chest with the same spot on the other side
Listening through one full inspiration and expiration at each site
Asking the client to cough and then re-listening over a gurgling area
Listening through the client’s hospital gown to keep the client warm
optionRationales: Incorrect. Side-to-side comparison is correct technique for detecting asymmetry.
Incorrect. A full breath at each spot is needed to judge timing and adventitious sounds.
Incorrect. Re-listening after a cough helps tell rhonchi from crackles.
Correct. Fabric muffles and distorts breath sounds; the stethoscope belongs on bare skin.
questions.rationale: Accurate auscultation uses the diaphragm of the stethoscope on bare skin, compares side to side, and listens through a full inspiration and expiration at each site. Clothing creates rustling and muffling that can hide adventitious sounds or mimic crackles. When a sound is heard, asking the client to cough and re-listening helps separate sounds that clear (rhonchi) from those that do not (crackles, wheezes). Keeping the client warm is a kind goal, which makes the gown option tempting, but warmth can be maintained by exposing one area at a time.
questions.takeaway: Auscultate on bare skin, side to side, through a full breath at each site.
questions.hintContent: Picture what fabric does to sound traveling to the stethoscope.
questions.hintStrategy: “Requires correction” means find the one incorrect action among correct ones.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with pneumonia reports a sharp pain in the right lower chest that gets worse with each deep breath and cough. Which additional finding would the nurse most expect?
options: A loud, high-pitched crowing sound heard on inspiration
A localized grating sound on both inspiration and expiration
Medium-pitched sounds with equal phases beside the sternum
Musical wheezes heard throughout all of the lung fields
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stridor arises from the upper airway, not from inflamed pleura.
Correct. Pleuritic pain from inflamed pleura is typically accompanied by a pleural friction rub in one spot.
Incorrect. These are normal bronchovesicular sounds and do not explain pleuritic pain.
Incorrect. Diffuse wheezes reflect narrowed airways, not inflamed pleura in one area.
questions.rationale: Pleuritic chest pain is sharp and worsens with breathing or coughing because inflamed pleural layers rub together as the lung moves. That rubbing produces a pleural friction rub: a grating, leathery sound heard over a localized area on both inspiration and expiration that does not clear with coughing. Pneumonia is a common cause. Wheezes are tempting because they are a familiar adventitious sound, but they come from narrowed airways and would not be localized to the painful spot.
questions.takeaway: Sharp pain with breathing plus a localized grating sound means inflamed pleura — a friction rub.
questions.hintContent: Link the type of pain to the structure that is inflamed, then to the sound it makes.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the finding that shares a cause with the symptom in the stem.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with pneumonia has had a falling SpO₂ for several hours despite oxygen therapy. Which findings indicate that the client’s compensation is failing (late hypoxia)? Select all that apply.
options: Respiratory rate increasing from 18 to 28/min
Heart rate decreasing from 124 to 54/min
New restlessness and picking at the bed linens
Bluish discoloration of the lips and tongue
Responds only to a firm shoulder shake
Blood pressure falling to 80/46 mm Hg
optionRationales: Incorrect. Tachypnea is an early compensatory response to hypoxia.
Correct. Bradycardia in a hypoxic client means the heart itself is running short of oxygen.
Incorrect. Restlessness is an early sign that the brain senses low oxygen.
Correct. Central cyanosis appears late, once oxygenation is severely impaired.
Correct. Progression to stupor reflects late, decompensated hypoxia.
Correct. Hypotension is a late sign that compensatory mechanisms are failing.
questions.rationale: Early hypoxia is the body compensating: restlessness, anxiety, irritability, tachycardia, tachypnea, and often a rise in blood pressure. Late hypoxia is compensation failing: bradycardia, hypotension, central cyanosis, and confusion progressing to stupor. A memory aid is that early hypoxia is “restless and fast,” while late hypoxia is “blue, slow, and low.” Tachypnea is the most tempting wrong choice because it is clearly abnormal, but it shows the body is still fighting back. Late signs call for a rapid response.
questions.takeaway: Early hypoxia is restless and fast; late hypoxia is blue, slow, and low.
questions.hintContent: Decide which findings show the body still fighting and which show it giving out.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort SATA options by a single principle — here, compensating versus decompensating.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nurse in an emergency department triages a 26-year-old client with a history of asthma. Which findings indicate severe respiratory distress? Select all that apply.
options: Sitting forward with hands braced on the knees
A newly hoarse, raspy voice
Neck muscles tightening with each breath
Soft, low-pitched breath sounds at the lung bases
Speaking only two or three words per breath
Speaking in full sentences while giving a history
optionRationales: Correct. The tripod position helps the chest expand and signals significant distress.
Correct. A hoarse voice reflects airway irritation or swelling and is a warning sign during a severe exacerbation.
Correct. Accessory muscle use shows that normal breathing muscles are not enough.
Incorrect. Vesicular sounds at the bases are a normal finding.
Correct. Being unable to finish a sentence indicates severe distress.
Incorrect. Full sentences indicate the client is moving adequate air.
questions.rationale: Before any test results return, the nurse can recognize severe respiratory distress from the client’s presentation: posture, ability to speak, voice, and effort. The tripod position, speaking only one to three words per breath, accessory muscle use, and a hoarse voice together describe a client in serious trouble. Speaking in full sentences means the client is moving more air, and vesicular sounds at the bases are normal. Students sometimes doubt the hoarse voice because it seems minor, but in an asthma exacerbation it reflects airway irritation and is a warning sign.
questions.takeaway: Posture, speech, voice, and effort reveal severe distress before any test does.
questions.hintContent: Use what you can see and hear from the doorway: how the client sits, talks, and works to breathe.
questions.hintStrategy: For SATA items, weigh each finding on its own — don’t stop after finding two correct ones.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nurse performs an admission assessment on a 70-year-old client. Which findings suggest long-standing (chronic) lung disease rather than an acute change? Select all that apply.
options: Clubbing of the fingernail beds
Inspiratory stridor audible without a stethoscope
Heart rate rising from 80 to 112/min over 2 hours
New restlessness that began this morning
A barrel-shaped chest
optionRationales: Correct. Clubbing develops over time with chronic hypoxemia, as in COPD.
