Incorrect. Stridor is an acute upper-airway emergency.
Incorrect. A rapid rise in heart rate is an acute compensatory response.
Incorrect. Sudden restlessness is an early sign of acute hypoxia, not a chronic finding.
Correct. A barrel chest reflects chronic air trapping, as in COPD.
questions.rationale: Some respiratory findings develop over months to years and become part of the client’s baseline. Clubbing of the nail beds indicates chronic hypoxemia, and a barrel chest reflects chronic air trapping; both are common in COPD. New restlessness, a rapidly rising heart rate, and stridor are acute changes that need immediate attention. Separating chronic from acute findings matters for prioritization, because a client with dramatic but chronic findings may be more stable than a client with a subtle new change.
questions.takeaway: Clubbing and barrel chest are chronic baseline findings; new restlessness, rising HR, and stridor are acute.
questions.hintContent: Ask how long each finding would take to develop.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify each option by time course: hours versus years.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client is scheduled for surgery tomorrow. While reviewing the home medication list, which medications should the nurse flag as able to depress the rate and depth of breathing? Select all that apply.
options: Lorazepam 1 mg at bedtime for anxiety
Albuterol inhaler 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed
Lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension
Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed
Zolpidem 5 mg at bedtime for insomnia
Oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed for back pain
optionRationales: Correct. Benzodiazepine sedatives can slow breathing, especially when combined with opioids.
Incorrect. Albuterol is a bronchodilator that opens airways; it does not depress breathing.
Incorrect. An antihypertensive does not suppress the drive to breathe.
Incorrect. Acetaminophen does not depress respiration.
Correct. Sedative-hypnotics add to respiratory depression, particularly with other sedating drugs.
Correct. Opioids depress the respiratory rate and depth.
questions.rationale: A respiratory medication history includes inhalers and how often they are used, and also any drugs that depress respiratory rate and depth — chiefly opioids and sedatives. Combining these drugs, or adding postoperative opioids to a home regimen, raises the risk of hypoventilation, CO₂ retention, and respiratory acidosis. Flagging them lets the provider and anesthesia team plan safely. Albuterol tempts some students because it is a respiratory drug, but it opens the airways rather than suppressing breathing.
questions.takeaway: Ask about opioids and sedatives in every respiratory history — they slow and shallow breathing.
questions.hintContent: For each drug, ask whether it affects the brain’s drive to breathe.
questions.hintStrategy: A drug “related to breathing” is not the same as a drug that depresses breathing — read the stem’s exact question.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing auscultation findings documented on several clients. Which findings require prompt follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Low-pitched gurgling in a client with bronchitis that clears after coughing
High-pitched crowing on inspiration in a client 1 hour after bronchoscopy
Bronchial sounds over the right lower lobe in a client who was admitted for a hip fracture
Barely audible breath sounds in a client with asthma who was wheezing loudly earlier
Soft, low-pitched sounds heard best at the bases of a healthy adult
optionRationales: Incorrect. Rhonchi that clear with coughing are expected with bronchitis and respond to airway clearance.
Correct. Stridor after bronchoscopy signals upper airway swelling — an emergency.
Correct. Bronchial sounds in a peripheral field suggest new consolidation that needs evaluation.
Correct. Diminished sounds after wheezing indicate failing airflow (silent chest).
Incorrect. Vesicular sounds at the bases are normal.
questions.rationale: Auscultation findings are interpreted in context. Stridor and a silent chest are airway emergencies; bronchial sounds over a peripheral field are a normal sound in the wrong place and suggest new consolidation, such as pneumonia, in a client admitted for an unrelated problem. Rhonchi that clear with coughing in a client with bronchitis are expected and are managed with coughing and deep breathing. The rhonchi option tempts students because any adventitious sound seems abnormal, but abnormal-and-expected is different from new-and-dangerous.
questions.takeaway: Stridor, a silent chest, and a normal sound in the wrong place need prompt follow-up.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each finding fits the client’s known condition or signals something new.
questions.hintStrategy: “Prompt follow-up” items reward separating expected abnormal findings from unexpected ones.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: An RN is working with an assistive personnel (AP) on a respiratory unit. Which tasks can the RN delegate to the AP? Select all that apply.
options: Deciding whether a client’s shortness of breath has improved
Counting and recording respirations for a stable postoperative client
Measuring and reporting the SpO₂ of a stable client with pneumonia
Helping a stable client with COPD sit upright for breakfast
Teaching a client how to use a new peak flow meter
Auscultating lung sounds after a client’s nebulizer treatment
optionRationales: Incorrect. Evaluating a client’s response is an RN responsibility.
Correct. Routine respiratory-rate measurement on a stable client may be delegated.
Correct. Collecting routine vital signs and SpO₂ on a stable client is within AP scope; the RN interprets the data.
Correct. Positioning a stable client is a basic care task an AP can perform.
Incorrect. Client teaching requires RN knowledge and cannot be delegated to an AP.
Incorrect. Auscultation is an assessment that requires the RN.
questions.rationale: Assistive personnel may collect vital signs, including SpO₂ and respiratory rate, and perform basic care such as positioning stable clients; the RN remains responsible for interpreting what is reported. Assessment (such as auscultation), evaluation of a client’s response, and teaching require RN judgment and cannot be delegated. Auscultation after a treatment is tempting because it seems like a simple data-collection step, but listening to lung sounds is an assessment that requires the RN to interpret the findings.
questions.takeaway: APs collect data and give basic care for stable clients; RNs assess, teach, and evaluate.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each task needs clinical judgment or is a routine, standardized task.
questions.hintStrategy: In delegation items, eliminate anything involving assessment, teaching, evaluation, or an unstable client.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client is admitted with a right-sided pneumothorax. Which assessment findings would the nurse expect on the right side of the chest? Select all that apply.
options: Diminished or absent breath sounds
Less chest movement than on the left
Bronchial breath sounds over the lower lobe
Fine crackles late in inspiration
Increased tactile fremitus
Decreased or absent tactile fremitus
optionRationales: Correct. Little air moves through the collapsed lung, so breath sounds are reduced or absent.
Correct. The collapsed lung does not expand, so that side rises less.
Incorrect. Bronchial sounds in a peripheral field indicate consolidation.
Incorrect. Crackles reflect fluid or collapsed alveoli popping open, not a pneumothorax.
Incorrect. Increased fremitus indicates consolidation, not air in the pleural space.
Correct. Air in the pleural space dampens vibration, so fremitus is decreased or absent.
questions.rationale: Air in the pleural space removes the negative pressure that holds the lung expanded, so the lung collapses. The nurse expects asymmetric chest expansion, with the affected side moving less, diminished or absent breath sounds, and decreased or absent tactile fremitus because vibration travels poorly through air. Increased fremitus and bronchial sounds are the findings of consolidation, the most commonly confused pattern. Remember the rule: solid lung carries sound and vibration better; air carries them worse.
questions.takeaway: Pneumothorax: decreased fremitus, decreased breath sounds, decreased chest rise on the affected side.
questions.hintContent: Think about how well vibration passes through air compared with solid tissue.
questions.hintStrategy: Contrast the look-alike condition (consolidation) and eliminate its findings.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client using a morphine patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump 8 hours after abdominal surgery has a respiratory rate of 8/min with shallow breaths. The client opens the eyes only to a loud voice and falls back asleep mid-sentence. SpO₂ is 92% on 2 L/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Stimulate the client by name and touch and support the airway
Increase the oxygen flow rate to 6 L/min by nasal cannula
Call the provider to report the low rate and heavy sedation
Recheck the sedation level and respiratory rate in 15 minutes
optionRationales: Correct. Bradypnea with heavy sedation means opioid-induced hypoventilation; rousing the client and keeping the airway open come first, before any call or recheck.
Incorrect. Extra oxygen does not correct hypoventilation and can hide rising CO₂ behind a better SpO₂.
Incorrect. The provider must be notified, but the nurse first stays to rouse the client and support the airway; calling first leaves the airway unprotected.
Incorrect. Monitoring sedation is appropriate, but the client is already dangerously sedated; waiting 15 minutes delays action in an emergency.
questions.rationale: Opioids depress the rate and depth of breathing. A rate below 10/min is bradypnea, and slow, shallow breathing is hypoventilation — too little air reaches the alveoli, so CO₂ builds up and respiratory acidosis develops. With heavy sedation, the first action is to stimulate the client and support the airway, then notify the provider and follow the opioid-reversal protocol. Turning up the oxygen is tempting because the SpO₂ is lower than ideal, but it does not fix the ventilation problem and can mask a climbing CO₂.
questions.takeaway: Opioid-induced bradypnea with heavy sedation: rouse the client and support the airway before anything else.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether the problem is getting oxygen in or getting air moving in and out.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the action that directly reverses the life-threatening problem, not one that improves a number.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A nurse on a medical step-down unit is caring for four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client receiving hospice care for end-stage heart failure who has had Cheyne-Stokes breathing for 2 days
A client with diabetic ketoacidosis on an insulin infusion whose deep, rapid breathing is slowing
A client with a head injury who has new crescendo–decrescendo breathing with apnea and a dilated pupil
A client with an anxiety disorder who is breathing 24/min with an SpO₂ of 99% on room air
optionRationales: Incorrect. This pattern is known, long-standing, and consistent with the client’s goals of care.
Incorrect. Kussmaul breathing easing as the acidosis is treated suggests improvement.
Correct. New Cheyne-Stokes breathing with a pupil change suggests rising intracranial pressure — an acute deterioration.
Incorrect. Mild tachypnea with normal oxygenation is less urgent than a neurologic decline.
questions.rationale: Cheyne-Stokes respirations — breaths that grow deeper and faster, then slower and shallower, followed by apnea — are associated with heart failure, increased intracranial pressure, and drug overdose. The meaning depends on context: in a client with a head injury, a new Cheyne-Stokes pattern plus a newly dilated pupil signals rising intracranial pressure and possible herniation, requiring immediate assessment and notification. The hospice client is the tempting choice because the pattern is identical, but it is established and expected. Kussmaul breathing that is slowing during treatment for DKA indicates the acidosis is improving.
questions.takeaway: The same breathing pattern can be expected in one client and an emergency in another — weigh what is new.
questions.hintContent: Identify which client’s pattern is new and paired with another sign of decline.
questions.hintStrategy: Acute change in an unstable condition beats a chronic or expected pattern.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client is 2 days postoperative after a laparoscopic colectomy. Pain is 2/10, and the client is taking shallow breaths and has not used the incentive spirometer. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), RR 22/min, SpO₂ 92% on room air, and breath sounds are diminished at both bases. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask the provider to prescribe an antibiotic for the fever
Coach deep breathing and incentive spirometry, then reassess
Give acetaminophen to bring down the temperature of 37.9°C
Apply oxygen at 4 L/min and continue to monitor the SpO₂
optionRationales: Incorrect. A low-grade fever with diminished bases fits atelectasis; there is no evidence of infection yet.
Correct. Pain is controlled, so the nurse targets the cause of the atelectasis — shallow breathing — with lung-expansion measures.
Incorrect. Treating the low-grade fever does not reopen the collapsed alveoli causing it.
Incorrect. Oxygen without lung expansion leaves the cause untreated, and this flow requires a prescription.
questions.rationale: Atelectasis begins when something reduces deep breathing or blocks an airway — pain, anesthesia, immobility, or mucus. Air behind the blockage is absorbed, alveoli collapse, and the client develops diminished breath sounds or crackles at the bases, tachypnea, a falling SpO₂, and often a low-grade fever. Because this client’s pain is already controlled, the nurse treats the cause directly with deep breathing and incentive spirometry, then reassesses. The antibiotic is tempting because of the fever, but early postoperative low-grade fever with diminished bases points to atelectasis, not pneumonia.
questions.takeaway: Shallow breathing after surgery causes atelectasis — reexpand the lungs with deep breathing and incentive spirometry.
questions.hintContent: Check whether pain is the barrier this time, then look for what the client isn’t doing.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the independent action that treats the cause rather than a symptom such as the fever.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: An AP lowered the head of the bed flat to change the linens of a client with heart failure. A few minutes later the client is gasping, says, “I can’t breathe lying down,” and has an SpO₂ of 90% (95% earlier). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Call the provider to request an additional diuretic dose
Auscultate the lungs with the client lying flat
Increase the oxygen flow rate to raise the SpO₂ above 95%
Raise the head of the bed to high-Fowler’s position
optionRationales: Incorrect. The provider may need to be informed, but repositioning relieves this client’s distress immediately.
Incorrect. Keeping the client flat for assessment prolongs the cause of the distress.
Incorrect. Positioning is the least invasive effective action; changing flow requires a prescription.
Correct. Orthopnea is relieved by sitting upright, which lowers the diaphragm and redistributes lung fluid.
questions.rationale: Orthopnea is difficulty breathing when lying flat. In the supine position abdominal organs push up on the diaphragm and fluid spreads across the lungs; sitting upright relieves both. The fastest, least invasive effective action is to raise the head of the bed, then reassess and report as needed. Assessing first is the tempting rule, but here the cause is obvious and easily reversed, so the nurse corrects it before gathering more data.
questions.takeaway: Orthopnea is relieved by sitting up — reposition first when lying flat caused the distress.
questions.hintContent: Ask what changed just before the distress started.
questions.hintStrategy: When a simple nursing action will reverse the cause, choose it over options needing orders.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with obstructive sleep apnea is 1 night postoperative after a knee arthroplasty and received oral oxycodone 2 hours ago. The AP reports loud snoring with pauses of about 20 seconds, during which the SpO₂ falls to 84%. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula and let the client sleep
Notify the provider about the episodes of oxygen desaturation
Wake the client and raise the head of the bed, then reassess
Document the pattern as the client’s usual sleep apnea
optionRationales: Incorrect. Oxygen may raise the SpO₂, but it does not reverse the airway obstruction or hypoventilation, and letting the client sleep allows the apnea to continue.
Incorrect. The provider should be notified, but the nurse first restores breathing at the bedside; calling first delays correcting the apnea.
Correct. Arousing the client restores breathing effort, and elevating the head opens the airway in a client with sleep apnea on opioids.
Incorrect. Pauses with SpO₂ dropping to 84% after an opioid are a dangerous change, not baseline.
questions.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnea already causes pauses in breathing, and opioids further slow breathing and relax the upper airway. That combination places the client at high risk for hypoventilation and apnea, especially at night. The nurse wakes the client to restore breathing effort, raises the head of the bed, reassesses rate, SpO₂, and sedation level, and notifies the provider. Documenting the pattern as usual is tempting because the client has a known diagnosis, but desaturation to 84% after an opioid is a new and dangerous change.
questions.takeaway: Sleep apnea plus opioids: rouse, raise the head of the bed, and reassess when pauses cause desaturation.
questions.hintContent: Think about what the opioid adds to the client’s existing breathing problem.
questions.hintStrategy: A known diagnosis doesn’t make a new, worse finding “baseline.”

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: Late in the evening, a client with pneumonia presses the call light and says, “I can’t catch my breath.” RR is 22/min and SpO₂ is 97% on 2 L/min. The client is sitting up and speaking in full sentences. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Assess breath sounds and effort, and have the client rate the dyspnea
Coach pursed-lip breathing and recheck the client in 15 minutes
Move the probe to another finger to confirm the SpO₂ reading
Increase the oxygen to 4 L/min to make the client comfortable
optionRationales: Correct. Dyspnea is subjective; the nurse assesses the symptom and the respiratory system rather than relying on the SpO₂ alone.
Incorrect. Pursed-lip breathing is a helpful independent action, but intervening before assessing could miss the cause of the new dyspnea.
Incorrect. Confirming the reading is reasonable, but it only checks a number; the client’s report needs a full respiratory assessment.
Incorrect. Changing flow without assessment and a prescription treats a number, not the client.
questions.rationale: Dyspnea — labored breathing or shortness of breath — is what the client feels, so it is subjective data that the nurse must take seriously. A normal SpO₂ does not rule out a problem: the client could be tiring, retaining CO₂, or developing a new complication. The nurse assesses work of breathing, listens to the lungs, and asks the client to rate the dyspnea and describe what makes it better or worse. Coaching pursed-lip breathing is tempting because it is a helpful independent action, but intervening before assessing skips the step that finds the cause.
questions.takeaway: Dyspnea is subjective — assess the client and the symptom, not just the oximeter.
questions.hintContent: Ask what kind of data the client’s statement is and how the nurse measures it.
questions.hintStrategy: When a stable client reports a symptom, assess before you act or reassure.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 19-year-old client with asthma is brought to the student health center breathing 30/min and reports tingling in the fingers. The roommate says, “She’s having a panic attack — give her a paper bag.” The nurse hears expiratory wheezes bilaterally, and SpO₂ is 88% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Have the client breathe slowly into a paper bag for several minutes
Coach slow breathing to correct the client’s respiratory alkalosis
Sit the client upright and assess for accessory muscle use
Apply oxygen per protocol and prepare the prescribed rescue inhaler
optionRationales: Incorrect. Rebreathing exhaled air in a hypoxemic client lowers oxygen further and is dangerous.
Incorrect. Coaching alone does not treat airway narrowing and hypoxemia.
Incorrect. Upright positioning helps and accessory muscle use is worth noting, but wheezes and an SpO₂ of 88% already confirm hypoxemia; more assessment delays treatment.
Correct. Wheezes with an SpO₂ of 88% point to an asthma exacerbation causing hypoxemia, which must be treated first with oxygen and a bronchodilator.
questions.rationale: Hyperventilation from anxiety blows off CO₂ and causes respiratory alkalosis with tingling around the mouth and fingers, but rapid breathing is also how the body compensates for low oxygen. Bilateral wheezes and an SpO₂ of 88% show a narrowed-airway problem with hypoxemia, so the nurse treats this as an asthma exacerbation: apply oxygen per protocol and give the prescribed rescue bronchodilator. The paper bag is the dangerous trap — assuming “panic” before ruling out hypoxia can kill a client whose fast breathing is a response to low oxygen.
questions.takeaway: Never assume fast breathing is anxiety until hypoxemia has been ruled out.
questions.hintContent: Look for objective data that confirm or contradict the roommate’s explanation.
questions.hintStrategy: When a benign explanation competes with a dangerous one, treat the dangerous one first.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a client with long-standing COPD. Which finding requires the nurse’s priority action?
options: Clubbed fingernails that the client says have looked this way for years
New retractions between the ribs with bluish lips and an SpO₂ of 82%
A barrel-shaped chest noted on every previous visit
Pursed-lip breathing while walking from the bedroom to the kitchen
optionRationales: Incorrect. Clubbing is a chronic sign of long-standing hypoxemia, not an acute change.
Correct. New retractions, cyanosis, and a very low SpO₂ indicate an acute worsening of gas exchange.
Incorrect. A barrel chest reflects chronic air trapping and is the client’s baseline.
Incorrect. Pursed-lip breathing is a helpful technique the client uses to keep airways open.
questions.rationale: In COPD, alveolar damage limits gas exchange, leading to CO₂ retention and decreased blood oxygen. Over years, clients develop chronic signs such as clubbing and a barrel chest, and they may learn pursed-lip breathing. New retractions with cyanosis and an SpO₂ of 82% show the client’s gas exchange is acutely worse than baseline and require prompt action. Clubbing is tempting because it is a classic sign of hypoxemia, but it reflects years of low oxygen rather than today’s change.
questions.takeaway: In chronic lung disease, new retractions and cyanosis outrank long-standing clubbing or barrel chest.
questions.hintContent: Decide which finding is new compared with the client’s usual presentation.
questions.hintStrategy: New and worsening beats chronic and stable, even when the chronic finding looks dramatic.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply and rapidly at 34/min with a regular rhythm. An AP says, “Should I have her breathe into a bag or count slow breaths with her? She’s breathing way too fast.” Which response by the RN is best?
options: “No — her fast, deep breathing is blowing off acid, so we treat the cause instead.”
“Yes — coach her to breathe slowly so her carbon dioxide level stays normal.”
“Yes — a paper bag will help her rebreathe carbon dioxide and calm down.”
“No — she is hyperventilating from anxiety, so give her some quiet privacy.”
optionRationales: Correct. Kussmaul breathing compensates for metabolic acidosis by eliminating CO₂; slowing it would worsen the acidosis.
Incorrect. Slowing Kussmaul breathing would let CO₂ build up and drive the pH lower.
Incorrect. Rebreathing CO₂ in metabolic acidosis adds acid and is dangerous.
Incorrect. This is compensatory Kussmaul breathing from acidosis, not anxiety-driven hyperventilation.
questions.rationale: Kussmaul breathing is deep, rapid, and regular and occurs in metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis. The deep, fast exhalations eliminate CO₂ to raise the pH — the lungs are compensating for an acid problem the kidneys and insulin therapy must correct. Coaching slower breathing or rebreathing into a bag would let CO₂ rise and make the acidosis worse. The anxiety option is tempting because the rate is fast, but the pattern here is a deliberate compensation, not a panic response.
questions.takeaway: Kussmaul breathing is compensation for metabolic acidosis — treat the cause, never slow the breathing.
questions.hintContent: Ask what the deep, rapid breaths are doing to CO₂ and why the body would want that.
questions.hintStrategy: When a sign is compensatory, eliminate options that try to suppress it.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: Two hours after receiving IV hydromorphone, a client reports a headache and is drowsy. RR is 9/min with shallow breaths. Which statement best describes the alteration in the client’s breathing?
options: Hyperventilation with loss of CO₂, leading toward respiratory alkalosis
Kussmaul breathing compensating for an underlying metabolic acidosis
Hypoventilation with retention of CO₂, leading toward respiratory acidosis
Biot respirations caused by an injury to the central nervous system
optionRationales: Incorrect. Hyperventilation is rapid and deep; this client is breathing slowly and shallowly.
Incorrect. Kussmaul breathing is deep and rapid, the opposite of this pattern.
Correct. Slow, shallow breathing moves too little air, so CO₂ builds up; headache and drowsiness are typical.
Incorrect. Biot breathing is irregular with apneic periods; this is a slow, regular, shallow pattern from an opioid.
questions.rationale: Hypoventilation is breathing that is too slow or too shallow, so too little air reaches the alveoli and CO₂ is retained, producing respiratory acidosis. Drowsiness and headache are typical symptoms of rising CO₂, and opioids are a common cause. A rate of 9/min is also below the bradypnea cutoff of 10/min. Hyperventilation is the tempting look-alike because both are “ventilation” words, but hyperventilation blows off CO₂ and causes alkalosis with tingling and lightheadedness.
questions.takeaway: Hypoventilation retains CO₂ (acidosis, drowsiness); hyperventilation blows it off (alkalosis, tingling).
questions.hintContent: Decide whether CO₂ is being retained or blown off at this rate and depth.
questions.hintStrategy: With look-alike terms, match the defining feature (rate and depth) before the label.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with heart failure told the clinic nurse last week that two pillows let her sleep comfortably. Today she says she has needed four pillows for the past three nights and has begun sleeping in a recliner. How should the nurse interpret this report?
options: Orthopnea is stable because the client still sleeps comfortably
Orthopnea is worsening, and the provider should be notified
Sleep apnea has developed and requires a sleep study first
Orthopnea is worsening, and the recliner is a safe way to manage it
optionRationales: Incorrect. The client is comfortable only because she now sleeps upright; going from two pillows to a recliner shows the orthopnea is getting worse.
Correct. Needing more pillows to breathe while lying down shows that orthopnea is increasing, which often reflects fluid buildup the provider must know about.
Incorrect. Needing to sit upright to breathe describes orthopnea, not obstructive pauses during sleep.
Incorrect. The interpretation is right, but sleeping upright only hides the symptom; the worsening must be reported so the cause can be treated.
questions.rationale: Orthopnea is difficulty breathing when lying flat, relieved by sitting up. Tracking the number of pillows the client needs is a simple way to measure it over time: going from two pillows to four and then to a recliner shows the condition is getting worse, often from increasing fluid in the lungs. The nurse reports this change to the provider. Accepting the recliner as a solution is tempting because the client sounds comfortable, but needing to sleep upright is an objective marker of decline that must be reported.
questions.takeaway: More pillows needed to sleep means worsening orthopnea — report it.
questions.hintContent: Compare last week’s pillow count with today’s and decide which direction the client is moving.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, compare current data with baseline before deciding whether the client improved.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with three fractured ribs is being discharged. The spouse asks, “Should I wrap his chest tightly with an elastic bandage so his ribs don’t move when he breathes?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Yes, wrapping will reduce his pain so he can breathe more comfortably.”
“A loose wrap is fine as long as he can still take a deep breath.”
“Yes, but loosen the wrap each time he uses his incentive spirometer.”
“Wrapping would limit his deep breaths and raise the risk of lung collapse.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Any comfort is outweighed by restricted chest expansion and atelectasis risk.
Incorrect. This sounds like a safe compromise, but any binding restricts chest expansion, and the client will breathe less deeply than he can.
Incorrect. Binding between spirometer sessions still limits expansion most of the day.
Correct. Binding the chest restricts expansion, encouraging shallow breathing and atelectasis.
questions.rationale: After rib fractures, pain causes splinting and shallow breathing, and shallow breathing leads to atelectasis. The goal is to let the client breathe deeply, so the plan is adequate pain control, splinting with a pillow when coughing, and incentive spirometry. Wrapping or binding the chest restricts expansion even further and increases the risk of collapse and pneumonia. The pain-relief option is tempting because it sounds supportive, but trading deep breaths for comfort is the wrong exchange.
questions.takeaway: Never bind the chest after rib fractures — control pain so the client can breathe deeply.
questions.hintContent: Think about what any tight wrap does to how much the chest can expand.
questions.hintStrategy: In teaching items, choose the response that corrects a harmful plan while explaining why.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A nurse is caring for four postoperative clients. Which client is at greatest risk for atelectasis?
options: A client after a lower abdominal surgery who walks the hallway four times a day
A client after a thyroidectomy who uses the incentive spirometer 10 times each hour
A client after upper abdominal surgery who splints the incision and refuses the spirometer
A client after a hip replacement who sits up in a chair and deep breathes hourly
optionRationales: Incorrect. Abdominal surgery raises risk, but a lower incision is less painful with breathing, and frequent walking promotes deep breaths and secretion clearance.
Incorrect. General anesthesia adds risk, but regular incentive spirometry reexpands alveoli and lowers it.
Correct. A painful upper abdominal incision with shallow breathing and no lung-expansion exercises is the classic path to alveolar collapse.
Incorrect. Major surgery and limited mobility add risk, but sitting upright and hourly deep breathing protect the lungs.
questions.rationale: Airway obstruction is the primary cause of atelectasis, and anything that reduces deep breathing or coughing — incisional pain, anesthesia, immobility, or mucus — allows airways to plug and alveoli to collapse. Upper abdominal incisions are especially painful with each breath, so clients splint and breathe shallowly. A client who also refuses the incentive spirometer has removed the main protection against collapse. The other clients have risk factors too, but they are walking, sitting up, deep breathing, or using the spirometer, which all lower risk.
questions.takeaway: Painful incisions plus shallow breathing and no lung-expansion exercises put clients at highest risk for atelectasis.
questions.hintContent: Look for the client who combines a reason to breathe shallowly with no lung-expansion activity.
questions.hintStrategy: For “greatest risk” items, choose the client with the most risk factors and the fewest protections.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis has been receiving an insulin infusion for 8 hours. Refer to the exhibit. Which conclusion is most accurate?

rows: pH 7.18, PaCO₂ 24 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 9 mEq/L
pH 7.27, PaCO₂ 30 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 14 mEq/L
pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 36 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 20 mEq/L

options: Kussmaul breathing is resolving as the metabolic acidosis is corrected
Respirations are slowing because the client is developing hypoventilation
The client has developed a new respiratory alkalosis from rapid breathing
The acidosis is worsening because the PaCO₂ has risen from 24 to 36 mm Hg
optionRationales: Correct. As bicarbonate and pH rise, the lungs no longer need to blow off as much CO₂, so breathing slows and becomes normal in depth.
Incorrect. PaCO₂ is returning to normal, not rising above 45 mm Hg, so this is not hypoventilation.
Incorrect. The pH is still slightly acidic and rising toward normal; there is no alkalosis.
Incorrect. The pH is rising toward normal; the PaCO₂ is rising because less respiratory compensation is needed.
questions.rationale: Kussmaul breathing — deep, rapid, regular respirations — is the lungs’ compensation for metabolic acidosis: blowing off CO₂ raises the pH. As insulin therapy corrects the ketoacidosis, HCO₃⁻ climbs toward normal and the need for compensation fades, so the rate slows, depth normalizes, and PaCO₂ rises back toward 35–45 mm Hg. Slowing breathing in this context is a sign of improvement. The hypoventilation option tempts students who see the rate falling, but hypoventilation would push PaCO₂ above normal rather than back into the normal range.
questions.takeaway: As metabolic acidosis is corrected, Kussmaul breathing slows and PaCO₂ returns toward normal.
questions.hintContent: Track all three columns together: breathing, glucose, and bicarbonate.
questions.hintStrategy: In trend exhibits, decide the direction of each value before choosing a conclusion.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A nurse is planning care for a client with pneumonia who becomes dyspneic with activity. Which nursing action requires a prescription from the provider?
options: Raising the head of the bed to high-Fowler’s position
Scheduling rest periods between bathing and ambulation
Coaching slow, deep breaths during periods of dyspnea
Increasing the oxygen flow rate from 2 to 4 L/min
optionRationales: Incorrect. Positioning to improve lung expansion is an independent nursing action.
Incorrect. Pacing activities to match tolerance is an independent nursing intervention.
Incorrect. Deep-breathing coaching is within the nurse’s independent scope.
Correct. Oxygen is a medication, so changing the flow rate requires a provider’s prescription or protocol.
questions.rationale: Many interventions that improve gas exchange and breathing patterns are independent — the nurse can perform them without an order. These include positioning, deep-breathing exercises, pursed-lip breathing, pacing activities and monitoring activity tolerance, promoting secretion clearance, and assisting with ADLs. Medications and changes to the oxygen prescription, however, require a provider’s order or an approved protocol. Students sometimes pick positioning because it seems “medical,” but it is a core independent nursing intervention.
questions.takeaway: Positioning, breathing coaching, and pacing are independent; changing oxygen flow needs a prescription.
questions.hintContent: Ask which option involves a medication.
questions.hintStrategy: For scope-of-practice items, treat oxygen like any other drug.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client is 1 day postoperative after an open cholecystectomy. Breath sounds are diminished at both bases and SpO₂ is 92% on room air. Which independent nursing actions should the nurse include to improve the client’s breathing pattern? Select all that apply.
options: Assist the client to walk in the hallway several times a day
Increase the oxygen to 4 L/min by nasal cannula
Apply a snug abdominal binder so the incision moves less with each breath
Coach the client to use the incentive spirometer 10 times every hour while awake
Teach the client to splint the incision with a pillow when coughing
optionRationales: Correct. Ambulation promotes deeper breathing and helps mobilize secretions.
Incorrect. Starting or changing oxygen requires a prescription or protocol; it is not an independent action.
Incorrect. Restricting movement with every breath encourages shallow breathing and worsens atelectasis; splinting only during coughing is the better approach.
Correct. Slow, deep breaths with the spirometer reexpand collapsed alveoli.
Correct. Splinting reduces incisional pain so the client can cough and breathe deeply.
questions.rationale: Postoperative atelectasis develops when pain, anesthesia, and immobility reduce deep breathing and coughing, so airways plug and alveoli collapse. Independent nursing actions that reverse this include deep breathing and incentive spirometry, early ambulation, and teaching the client to splint the incision so coughing hurts less. Oxygen is tempting because the SpO₂ is low, but it is a medication that requires a prescription and does not reopen collapsed alveoli by itself. Anything that restricts chest or abdominal movement makes shallow breathing worse.
questions.takeaway: Treat atelectasis with independent lung-expansion actions: incentive spirometry, ambulation, and splinted coughing.
questions.hintContent: For each option, ask whether it makes breaths deeper and whether the nurse can do it without an order.
questions.hintStrategy: When the stem says “independent,” eliminate anything that requires a prescription.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A college student is brought to the campus clinic during a panic attack. The student is breathing rapidly and deeply. Breath sounds are clear, and SpO₂ is 99% on room air. Which findings would the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
options: Numbness and tingling around the mouth
A PaCO₂ above 45 mm Hg on an arterial blood gas
Lightheadedness or dizziness
Drowsiness and a dull headache from CO₂ buildup
Tingling in the fingers
optionRationales: Correct. Blowing off CO₂ causes respiratory alkalosis, which produces perioral tingling.
Incorrect. Hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂ below 35, not above 45.
Correct. Low CO₂ from hyperventilation commonly causes lightheadedness.
Incorrect. These are signs of CO₂ retention from hypoventilation, the opposite problem.
Correct. Respiratory alkalosis often causes tingling in the hands and fingers.
questions.rationale: Hyperventilation is rapid, deep breathing that blows off too much CO₂, lowering PaCO₂ and causing respiratory alkalosis. Typical symptoms include tingling around the mouth and in the fingers and lightheadedness. Because the lungs are clear and SpO₂ is normal, anxiety is the likely driver in this client. The drowsiness-and-headache option tempts students who remember that CO₂ changes cause symptoms but mix up the direction: those symptoms come from CO₂ retention in hypoventilation.
questions.takeaway: Hyperventilation → low CO₂ → respiratory alkalosis → tingling and lightheadedness.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether CO₂ is rising or falling, then match the symptoms.
questions.hintStrategy: Look-alike items: pair each symptom with its direction of CO₂ change before selecting.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A charge nurse reviews clients receiving opioids on a surgical unit. Which clients are at increased risk for opioid-induced hypoventilation? Select all that apply.
options: A client who has used oxycodone for 1 week with stable sedation and RR 16/min
A client who walks the hallway hourly and uses the incentive spirometer
A client receiving IV morphine who also takes lorazepam at bedtime
A client with COPD who retains CO₂ at baseline
A 72-year-old client with obstructive sleep apnea in the first night after surgery
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stable sedation and a normal rate after a week suggest tolerance of the dose.
Incorrect. Frequent activity and deep breathing lower the risk of hypoventilation.
Correct. Combining an opioid with a sedative adds to respiratory depression.
Correct. Opioids further depress breathing in a client who already retains CO₂.
Correct. Sleep apnea already causes pauses in breathing, and opioids worsen airway relaxation and respiratory depression.
questions.rationale: Hypoventilation — breathing too slowly or shallowly — causes CO₂ retention and respiratory acidosis, and opioids are a leading cause. Risk climbs when other factors already depress breathing or obstruct the airway: obstructive sleep apnea, older age, concurrent sedatives such as benzodiazepines, and chronic CO₂ retention from COPD. For these clients the nurse checks rate, depth, and sedation level before every dose, keeps the head of the bed up, uses continuous monitoring as ordered, and avoids extra sedating drugs. The stable client on oxycodone tempts students because all opioids carry risk, but this client shows no added risk factors and stable findings.
questions.takeaway: Sleep apnea, sedatives, older age, and CO₂ retention multiply the risk of opioid-induced hypoventilation.
questions.hintContent: Look for anything that already slows breathing or narrows the airway before the opioid is added.
questions.hintStrategy: For “at increased risk” SATA items, select clients with stacked risk factors, not merely the drug.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with long-standing COPD is admitted for a routine procedure. Which findings would the nurse expect as a result of the client’s impaired gas exchange? Select all that apply.
options: Clubbed nail beds
A PaCO₂ above 45 mm Hg
Deep, rapid, regular Kussmaul respirations
Retractions between the ribs during breathing
A PaCO₂ below 35 mm Hg
optionRationales: Correct. Clubbing reflects oxygen levels that have been low for a long time.
Correct. Alveolar damage limits CO₂ removal, causing CO₂ retention.
Incorrect. Kussmaul breathing occurs in metabolic acidosis, not chronic COPD.
Correct. Retractions show the extra effort needed to breathe with damaged lungs.
Incorrect. Low CO₂ reflects hyperventilation, not the CO₂ retention typical of COPD.
questions.rationale: In COPD, alveolar damage limits the exchange of O₂ and CO₂, so CO₂ is retained and blood oxygen falls. Over time, the client may show retractions from the effort of breathing, cyanosis, and clubbed nail beds from chronic low oxygen. A PaCO₂ above 45 mm Hg (hypercarbia) fits CO₂ retention. Kussmaul respirations are tempting because they are a named abnormal pattern, but they reflect the lungs compensating for metabolic acidosis, not a gas-exchange disease.
questions.takeaway: COPD → CO₂ retention and low O₂ → retractions, cyanosis, clubbing, PaCO₂ above 45.
questions.hintContent: Ask which direction CO₂ moves when damaged alveoli cannot exchange gas.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that describe a different disease process, even if they are abnormal.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nurse on a medical-surgical unit observes the breathing patterns of several clients. Which findings require the nurse to notify the provider promptly? Select all that apply.
options: A client with a subarachnoid hemorrhage who now has shallow, irregular breaths with random pauses
A client with panic disorder whose rapid breathing and finger tingling resolved after coached slow breathing
A client with emphysema who uses pursed-lip breathing while walking back from the bathroom
A client with new-onset diabetes who has fruity breath and deep, rapid, regular breathing
A client admitted after a sleeping-pill overdose who has crescendo–decrescendo breathing with pauses
optionRationales: Correct. New Biot breathing signals worsening central nervous system function.
Incorrect. The hyperventilation responded to an independent intervention and has resolved.
Incorrect. Pursed-lip breathing is an effective technique the client is using appropriately.
Correct. Kussmaul breathing indicates metabolic acidosis, which needs prompt treatment of the cause.
Correct. Cheyne-Stokes respirations can accompany drug overdose and signal serious respiratory depression.
questions.rationale: The named breathing patterns each point to a cause. Biot respirations — shallow breathing with irregular apneic periods — occur in central nervous system disorders and signal a worsening brain condition. Cheyne-Stokes respirations — crescendo–decrescendo cycles with apnea — occur with heart failure, increased intracranial pressure, and drug overdose. Kussmaul respirations — deep, rapid, and regular — indicate metabolic acidosis, such as diabetic ketoacidosis; the breathing should not be slowed, but the acidosis needs urgent treatment. Pursed-lip breathing and resolved hyperventilation are tempting because they involve altered breathing, but both show effective self-management or an intervention that worked.
questions.takeaway: Biot, new Cheyne-Stokes, and Kussmaul patterns each point to a serious cause the provider must treat.
questions.hintContent: Name each pattern, then recall the condition it signals.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate abnormal patterns that signal disease from altered breathing that reflects a helpful technique.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nurse is classifying the oxygenation problems of several clients. Which clients have an alteration primarily in airway patency? Select all that apply.
options: A client with emphysema whose damaged alveoli limit O₂ and CO₂ exchange
A client with heart failure who has Cheyne-Stokes respirations
A child who inhaled a small toy that lodged in a bronchus
A client with acute bronchitis whose inflamed airway lining has swollen
A client with thick mucus plugs in the bronchi after pneumonia
optionRationales: Incorrect. Alveolar damage is a gas-exchange alteration, not an airway blockage.
Incorrect. Cheyne-Stokes is an alteration in respiratory pattern.
Correct. A foreign body obstructs airflow through the airway.
Correct. Inflammation swells the lining and narrows the passage.
Correct. Thick sputum physically blocks the airway.
questions.rationale: Alterations in oxygenation can be described in three areas: gas exchange (is O₂ crossing into the blood and CO₂ leaving?), airway patency (is the airway open?), and respiratory pattern (is the rate, depth, and rhythm normal?). Thick sputum, a foreign body, and inflammation of the airway lining all block or narrow the airway, so they are airway-patency problems — and airway obstruction is the primary cause of atelectasis. Emphysema is the tempting distractor because it is an obstructive disease, but its defining problem in this framework is alveolar damage limiting gas exchange.
questions.takeaway: Airway patency asks “Is the tube open?” — mucus, foreign bodies, and inflammation close it.
questions.hintContent: Picture the airway as a tube; ask whether anything is blocking or narrowing it.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the three-category framework to sort each client before selecting.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client with pneumonia who reports shortness of breath. Which data are subjective? Select all that apply.
options: “I feel like I can’t get enough air.”
SpO₂ of 91% on room air
The client says breathing is worse when lying flat
The client rates the breathlessness as 7 on a 0–10 scale
Respiratory rate of 26/min
Neck muscles tightening with each breath
optionRationales: Correct. The client’s description of breathlessness is subjective data.
Incorrect. A device measurement is objective data.
Correct. A report of orthopnea from the client is subjective.
Correct. A self-rating of dyspnea is the client’s report and therefore subjective.
Incorrect. A counted rate is objective, measurable data.
Incorrect. Accessory muscle use is observed by the nurse and is objective.
questions.rationale: Dyspnea is labored breathing or shortness of breath — something the client feels — so it is subjective data. The nurse collects it by asking the client to describe it, rate it, and identify what makes it better or worse; a report of breathlessness when lying flat (orthopnea) is also subjective. Respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, and SpO₂ are objective because the nurse counts, observes, or measures them. Students sometimes mark the 0–10 rating as objective because it is a number, but the number comes from the client’s own perception.
questions.takeaway: What the client feels and reports is subjective — even when it is expressed as a number.
questions.hintContent: Ask who generated each piece of data: the client or the nurse’s senses and devices.
questions.hintStrategy: A number does not make data objective; the source does.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 24-year-old client is being treated in the emergency department for a severe asthma exacerbation. Refer to the exhibit. Which action should the nurse take first?

rows: pH 7.49, PaCO₂ 31 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L, PaO₂ 64 mm Hg
Faint wheezes; drowsy, slow to answer
pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 44 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L, PaO₂ 58 mm Hg

options: Document that the ABG has returned to normal limits
Notify the provider immediately that the client is tiring
Allow the client to rest because the respiratory rate has improved
Repeat the ABG in 1 hour to confirm the trend
optionRationales: Incorrect. The numbers are “normal” only because CO₂ is rising toward failure; the trend and the client’s condition are worsening.
Correct. A CO₂ that has climbed from 31 to 44 with drowsiness and fainter wheezes means the client can no longer blow off CO₂ — impending respiratory failure.
Incorrect. A slower rate with drowsiness reflects exhaustion, not improvement.
Incorrect. Waiting an hour risks respiratory arrest in a client who is already decompensating.
questions.rationale: Early in an asthma attack the client breathes fast and blows off CO₂, so PaCO₂ is low and pH is alkalotic. As the client tires, CO₂ is no longer removed and begins to climb; a “normal” or rising CO₂ in an asthma exacerbation is ominous. Here the CO₂ rose from 31 to 44 while the client became drowsy, the wheezes faded, and the PaO₂ and SpO₂ fell — signs of impending respiratory failure that require immediate provider notification. Documenting a normal ABG is the trap: each value is within range, but the trend shows the client is losing the fight.
questions.takeaway: In an asthma attack, a normal or rising PaCO₂ with drowsiness means the client is tiring — escalate now.
questions.hintContent: Compare 0930 with 0800 for every column, not just whether 0930 values are “normal.”
questions.hintStrategy: In trend exhibits, interpret the direction of change in context, not single values in isolation.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 70-year-old client rescued from a house fire reports a throbbing headache and is confused. RR is 24/min, and SpO₂ reads 99% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply oxygen per protocol and anticipate a carboxyhemoglobin level
Reassure the client that the oxygen level is normal and observe
Move the probe to an earlobe to confirm the accuracy of the reading
Give acetaminophen for the headache and reassess in 1 hour
optionRationales: Correct. A standard oximeter cannot distinguish carbon monoxide from oxygen on hemoglobin, so the nurse treats suspected poisoning and anticipates co-oximetry.
Incorrect. The SpO₂ may be falsely normal with carbon monoxide poisoning; confusion and headache suggest tissue hypoxia.
Incorrect. A different site still cannot tell carbon monoxide from oxygen, so this delays treatment.
Incorrect. Treating the headache alone ignores a likely life-threatening cause.
questions.rationale: Carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin, and a standard pulse oximeter cannot tell carbon monoxide from oxygen on hemoglobin. As a result, SpO₂ may read normal or even high while the client is severely hypoxic, which is why headache and confusion after smoke inhalation are taken seriously. The nurse applies oxygen per protocol and anticipates an ABG with co-oximetry to measure carboxyhemoglobin. Moving the probe is tempting because it is the standard fix for an unreliable reading, but no site can detect carbon monoxide.
questions.takeaway: After smoke exposure, a normal SpO₂ does not rule out carbon monoxide poisoning — treat and check carboxyhemoglobin.
questions.hintContent: Recall which situations make a pulse oximeter read falsely normal.
questions.hintStrategy: When a device reading conflicts with the client’s symptoms, ask whether the device has a known blind spot.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: One hour after a flexible bronchoscopy with a topical throat anesthetic, a client who is awake and alert says, “My mouth is so dry — can I please have some water?” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Offer small sips of cool water through a straw to moisten the mouth
Offer a few ice chips so the client can moisten the mouth slowly
Check that the gag reflex has returned before giving anything by mouth
Give a throat lozenge to soothe the dryness and the sore throat
optionRationales: Incorrect. Even small sips can be aspirated if the gag reflex has not returned.
Incorrect. Ice chips melt into water that can be aspirated without a gag reflex.
Correct. The throat was numbed; until the gag reflex returns, any fluid could be aspirated.
Incorrect. A lozenge is something by mouth and is a choking risk while the throat is numb.
questions.rationale: Bronchoscopy passes a scope into the airways, and the throat is anesthetized so the client can tolerate it. Until the gag reflex returns, the client cannot protect the airway and could aspirate food, fluids, ice, or a lozenge. The nurse checks the gag reflex before offering anything by mouth. Ice chips are the most tempting option because they seem gentler than water, but they still enter the airway as fluid if the reflex is absent.
questions.takeaway: After bronchoscopy, nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns.
questions.hintContent: Think about what the topical anesthetic did to the client’s protective reflexes.
questions.hintStrategy: When every option offers something by mouth, look for the one that checks safety first.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with asthma calls the clinic and reports a peak flow reading of 210 L/min that has not improved 20 minutes after two puffs of albuterol. The client’s personal best is 500 L/min, and the client is speaking in short phrases. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give?
options: “Take two more puffs of albuterol and recheck your peak flow in an hour.”
“Call 911 or have someone take you to the emergency department now.”
“Follow the yellow-zone steps in your action plan and call back tonight.”
“Take your prescribed oral steroid now and call us back in an hour.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Waiting an hour in the red zone with breathlessness delays emergency care.
Correct. 210 L/min is 42% of personal best — the red zone — and not improving after rescue medicine, so the client needs emergency care.
Incorrect. Yellow zone is 50–79% of personal best; this reading is below 50%.
Incorrect. An oral steroid may be part of the action plan, but it takes hours to work; a red-zone reading with short-phrase speech needs emergency care now.
questions.rationale: Peak expiratory flow is compared with the client’s personal best. The green zone is 80% or more (good control), the yellow zone is 50–79% (use rescue medicine and follow the action plan), and the red zone is below 50%, a medical emergency. A reading of 210 L/min is 42% of 500, and it has not responded to albuterol; speaking only in short phrases confirms severe distress. The yellow-zone option is tempting because rescue medicine has been tried, but the number places the client in the red zone, which calls for emergency care.
questions.takeaway: Peak flow below 50% of personal best — especially after rescue medicine — means emergency care now.
questions.hintContent: Calculate the reading as a percentage of the client’s personal best.
questions.hintStrategy: For action-plan items, place the value in its zone before choosing the instruction.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A 27-year-old client is scheduled for a chest x-ray to evaluate a persistent cough. While the nurse prepares her, she says, “My period is about two weeks late.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Proceed because a chest x-ray delivers a very small dose of radiation
Remove her necklace and send her to radiology as scheduled
Place a lead shield over her abdomen and proceed with the x-ray
Hold the x-ray and notify the provider of the possible pregnancy
optionRationales: Incorrect. The nurse does not decide that the risk is acceptable; the provider needs this information first.
Incorrect. Removing metal is appropriate preparation, but it does not address the possible pregnancy.
Incorrect. Shielding seems protective, but deciding whether to proceed with a possible pregnancy belongs to the provider, who must be told before any radiation exposure.
Correct. Possible pregnancy must be reported before radiation exposure so the provider can decide how to proceed.
questions.rationale: Preparation for a chest x-ray includes removing metal from the chest area and asking about pregnancy, because radiation can harm a developing fetus. A late period is a possible pregnancy, and the nurse reports it to the provider before the test so the provider can decide whether to order a pregnancy test, shield, or change the plan. Proceeding because the dose is small is tempting, but that is a provider decision made with full information. Shielding the abdomen and proceeding is tempting too, but whether shielding is enough is also the provider’s decision.
questions.takeaway: Ask about pregnancy before any chest x-ray and report a possible pregnancy before exposure.
questions.hintContent: Recall the two standard safety checks before a chest x-ray.
questions.hintStrategy: When new information changes the risk of a procedure, hold it and inform the provider.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: Fifteen minutes after a radial arterial blood gas was drawn and pressure was held for 5 minutes, a client reports numbness in the fingers of that hand. The hand is pale and cool, and capillary refill is 5 seconds. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply a tight pressure dressing over the puncture site
Elevate the hand above the heart and recheck in 1 hour
Notify the provider of impaired circulation to the hand
Place a warm pack on the hand to improve circulation
optionRationales: Incorrect. Tight compression could further reduce arterial flow to the hand.
Incorrect. Elevation reduces arterial inflow, and waiting delays treatment of ischemia.
Correct. Pallor, coolness, numbness, and delayed refill after an arterial puncture indicate compromised arterial flow that needs prompt evaluation.
Incorrect. Warmth does not restore blocked arterial flow and can injure numb tissue.
questions.rationale: Arterial blood is under high pressure, so bleeding is the main risk after an ABG, and the nurse holds firm pressure for at least 5 minutes (10 minutes or more with anticoagulants). Afterward the nurse checks the site and the hand’s circulation — color, warmth, capillary refill, and pulse. A pale, cool, numb hand with delayed capillary refill suggests arterial flow is compromised, which requires prompt provider evaluation. A tight pressure dressing is tempting because it seems to protect the site, but it could worsen ischemia.
questions.takeaway: After an ABG, check the hand; pallor, coolness, numbness, or slow refill must be reported promptly.
questions.hintContent: Identify which structure the puncture affected and what these signs say about blood flow beyond it.
questions.hintStrategy: For possible ischemia, avoid any option that further restricts flow or delays evaluation.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: A nurse receives arterial blood gas results for four clients. Refer to the exhibit. Which client should the nurse address first?

rows: COPD, routine clinic visit, usual dyspnea
Postoperative day 1 on opioid PCA, difficult to arouse

options: Client Y, who is difficult to arouse on an opioid PCA
Client W, who has COPD and is at a routine clinic visit
Client X, who is anxious before surgery
Client Z, who has DKA and is on an insulin infusion
optionRationales: Correct. Uncompensated respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia and decreased responsiveness signals dangerous hypoventilation.
Incorrect. Normal pH with high CO₂ and high HCO₃⁻ is fully compensated respiratory acidosis — this client’s baseline.
Incorrect. Mild uncompensated respiratory alkalosis from anxiety is not immediately dangerous.
Incorrect. Partially compensated metabolic acidosis that is improving on insulin is less urgent than acute hypoventilation.
questions.rationale: Interpret each ABG in order: pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻, match, compensation, then oxygen. Client Y has a pH of 7.24 with a PaCO₂ of 66 and a normal HCO₃⁻ — uncompensated respiratory acidosis — plus hypoxemia and decreased responsiveness, a picture of opioid-induced hypoventilation that can progress to arrest. Client W is tempting because the CO₂ is high, but the normal pH and elevated HCO₃⁻ show long-standing, fully compensated respiratory acidosis. Acute, uncompensated, and symptomatic outranks chronic and compensated.
questions.takeaway: An acute, uncompensated acidosis with a declining level of consciousness outranks a compensated chronic ABG.
questions.hintContent: Interpret each ABG fully, then ask which client is acute and symptomatic.
questions.hintStrategy: Uncompensated and symptomatic beats compensated and baseline.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client has had persistent vomiting for 3 days and is admitted for dehydration. Refer to the exhibit. Which interpretation of the arterial blood gas is accurate?
options: Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis
Fully compensated metabolic alkalosis
Partially compensated respiratory acidosis
Partially compensated metabolic alkalosis
optionRationales: Incorrect. Respiratory alkalosis requires a low PaCO₂; this PaCO₂ is high.
Incorrect. Full compensation requires a pH back within 7.35–7.45; 7.50 is still alkalotic.
Incorrect. The pH is alkalotic, not acidotic, so this cannot be an acidosis.
Correct. pH and HCO₃⁻ are both high (same direction = metabolic), and the CO₂ is rising to compensate while pH is still abnormal.
questions.rationale: Work the steps. The pH of 7.50 is alkalosis. The PaCO₂ of 47 is on the acid side, so it does not match; the HCO₃⁻ of 34 is high (base) and matches, so the cause is metabolic — consistent with losing stomach acid through vomiting. Because the PaCO₂ has moved in the opposite direction (the lungs retaining CO₂ to compensate) but the pH is still abnormal, the result is partially compensated. Fully compensated is tempting because both values are abnormal, but full compensation requires a pH back inside 7.35–7.45.
questions.takeaway: Two abnormal values with an abnormal pH = partial compensation; a normal pH = full compensation.
questions.hintContent: Find which value matches the pH direction, then check whether pH is back in range.
questions.hintStrategy: ROME: in a metabolic problem, pH and HCO₃⁻ move in the same direction.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease comes to the nephrology clinic for a routine visit and reports feeling at baseline. Refer to the exhibit. Which interpretation of the arterial blood gas is accurate?
options: Fully compensated respiratory alkalosis
Fully compensated metabolic acidosis
Partially compensated metabolic acidosis
Uncompensated metabolic acidosis
optionRationales: Incorrect. A primary respiratory alkalosis would leave the pH on the alkaline side of 7.40.
Correct. The pH is normal but on the acid side of 7.40, HCO₃⁻ is low (matches acid), and CO₂ is low from respiratory compensation.
Incorrect. The pH is within 7.35–7.45, so compensation is complete, not partial.
Incorrect. Uncompensated means the PaCO₂ is normal and the pH abnormal; here both differ.
questions.rationale: When the pH is within 7.35–7.45 but both PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are abnormal, the imbalance is fully compensated, and the side of 7.40 on which the pH sits names the original problem. A pH of 7.36 sits on the acid side. The low HCO₃⁻ is an acid-side value that matches, so the primary problem is metabolic acidosis — consistent with kidneys that cannot retain bicarbonate. The low PaCO₂ is the lungs compensating. Respiratory alkalosis is the tempting look-alike because the CO₂ is low, but the pH on the acid side identifies acidosis as the original disorder.
questions.takeaway: With a normal pH and two abnormal values, the side of 7.40 tells you the original disorder.
questions.hintContent: Note which side of 7.40 the pH falls on before deciding which value is primary.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the 7.40 midpoint as a tiebreaker for fully compensated ABGs.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 61-year-old client with suspected COPD is scheduled for outpatient pulmonary function tests (PFTs) tomorrow. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the preparation?
options: “I won’t smoke beforehand, and I’ll follow the instructions about holding my inhalers.”
“I’ll take two extra puffs of my inhaler right before the test so I do my best.”
“I’ll stop all of my medicines, including my blood pressure pills, the night before.”
“I can’t eat or drink anything afterward until my gag reflex has fully come back.”
optionRationales: Correct. Smoking and inhaler use can alter results, so clients avoid smoking and follow inhaler-holding instructions.
Incorrect. Using an inhaler just before testing can change the results unless the provider instructs otherwise.
Incorrect. Holding some medicines is right, but only specified ones such as bronchodilators are held; stopping all medicines without instruction is unsafe.
Incorrect. That precaution applies after bronchoscopy, not after PFTs.
questions.rationale: Pulmonary function tests measure lung volumes and how quickly air moves out of the lungs; they help identify obstructive disease such as asthma and COPD. Because the client must breathe into a machine, the results depend on effort and on what has affected the airways beforehand, so clients avoid smoking and follow instructions about holding inhalers. The extra-puffs option is tempting because the client wants to perform well, but it would distort the results the provider needs. The gag-reflex option describes bronchoscopy, a commonly confused test.
questions.takeaway: Before PFTs: no smoking, and hold inhalers only as instructed.
questions.hintContent: Recall what the client actually does during a PFT and what could change the result.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that borrow precautions from a different procedure.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: In the endoscopy recovery area, a client recovering from procedural sedation is drowsy with a respiratory rate of 9/min. SpO₂ is 97% on 3 L/min by nasal cannula. Which data would best determine whether the client is ventilating adequately?
options: A continuous SpO₂ trend over the next hour
Heart rate and blood pressure every 15 minutes
PaCO₂ on an arterial blood gas
Capillary refill time in the fingers
optionRationales: Incorrect. SpO₂ reflects oxygen saturation and can stay normal on oxygen while CO₂ rises.
Incorrect. Vital signs are important but do not measure CO₂ removal.
Correct. PaCO₂ directly reflects how well the lungs are removing CO₂ — the measure of ventilation.
Incorrect. Capillary refill assesses peripheral perfusion, not ventilation.
questions.rationale: Ventilation is the movement of air in and out of the lungs, and its job includes removing CO₂. The only listed measure that directly reflects ventilation is PaCO₂: a value above 45 mm Hg (hypercarbia) means CO₂ is being retained. SpO₂ is tempting because it is continuous and easy, but it tells nothing about CO₂, and supplemental oxygen can keep it normal while the client hypoventilates. Pulse oximetry is a trend tool for oxygenation that must be correlated with the client’s assessment.
questions.takeaway: SpO₂ measures oxygenation; PaCO₂ measures ventilation.
questions.hintContent: Ask which value reflects carbon dioxide rather than oxygen.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the measurement to the exact question asked — here, ventilation, not oxygenation.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with sudden dyspnea is scheduled for a pulmonary ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) scan and asks what the test involves. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “A flexible scope will be passed into your airways to look for a blockage.”
“You’ll inhale one tracer and get another through your IV to compare airflow and blood flow.”
“A needle will be placed between your ribs to remove fluid from around the lung.”
“You’ll blow as hard and as fast as you can into a small meter several times in a row.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This describes bronchoscopy, not a V/Q scan.
Correct. A V/Q scan has two parts — an inhaled tracer for ventilation and an IV tracer for perfusion — to look for a mismatch such as a clot.
Incorrect. This describes thoracentesis.
Incorrect. This describes peak flow or pulmonary function testing.
questions.rationale: A pulmonary V/Q scan compares ventilation (air) with perfusion (blood) in each area of the lungs to look for a mismatch — for example, a region that is ventilated but not perfused because a clot blocks blood flow. The nurse explains the two parts: inhaling a tracer and receiving a tracer through an IV. The bronchoscopy option is tempting because it also “looks inside” the lungs, but it uses a scope rather than tracers and evaluates the airways themselves. Clear explanation reduces anxiety and improves cooperation.
questions.takeaway: A V/Q scan pairs an inhaled tracer with an IV tracer to compare airflow and blood flow.
questions.hintContent: Break the test name into its two letters and what each measures.
questions.hintStrategy: When options describe different procedures, match the description to the test named in the stem.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A nurse has just drawn a radial arterial blood gas from a client receiving oxygen at 3 L/min by nasal cannula. The client takes no anticoagulants. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Apply light pressure for 1 minute, then cover the site with a bandage
Note on the requisition that the client is on oxygen at 3 L/min
Check the hand’s color, warmth, capillary refill, and pulse
Have the client flex the wrist repeatedly to restore circulation
Hold firm, direct pressure on the site for at least 5 minutes
After pressure, check the site for bleeding or swelling
optionRationales: Incorrect. One minute of light pressure is not enough for an arterial puncture.
Correct. Oxygen values are interpreted in light of the oxygen the client was receiving.
Correct. Circulation beyond the puncture must be confirmed.
Incorrect. Movement can dislodge the clot and cause bleeding at the site.
Correct. Arterial blood is under high pressure; at least 5 minutes of pressure prevents bleeding and hematoma.
Correct. Bleeding is the main risk after an arterial puncture.
questions.rationale: ABGs are drawn from an artery, usually the radial artery, where blood is under high pressure, so bleeding is the main risk afterward. The nurse holds firm, direct pressure for at least 5 minutes (10 minutes or more for clients on anticoagulants), then checks the site and the circulation to the hand. The requisition must state whether the client is on room air or oxygen, and at what flow, because the oxygen values only make sense in context. The 1-minute option is tempting because it is what is done after a venous draw, but an artery needs much longer.
questions.takeaway: After an ABG: firm pressure ≥ 5 minutes (≥ 10 on anticoagulants), then check the site and the hand; note the oxygen on the requisition.
questions.hintContent: Think about how arterial pressure differs from venous pressure.
questions.hintStrategy: Don’t carry venipuncture habits over to arterial procedures.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A nurse reviews ABG results for several clients. Which results show that compensation has begun (partial or full)? Select all that apply.
options: pH 7.52, PaCO₂ 28 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 23 mEq/L
pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 17 mEq/L
pH 7.33, PaCO₂ 52 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 30 mEq/L
pH 7.31, PaCO₂ 33 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L
pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 48 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 32 mEq/L
optionRationales: Incorrect. Respiratory alkalosis with a normal HCO₃⁻ is uncompensated.
Incorrect. Metabolic acidosis with a normal PaCO₂ is uncompensated.
Correct. Respiratory acidosis with an elevated HCO₃⁻ — the kidneys are compensating (partially).
Correct. Metabolic acidosis with a low PaCO₂ — the lungs are partially compensating.
Correct. Normal pH with both values abnormal is fully compensated metabolic alkalosis (pH on the alkaline side of 7.40).
questions.rationale: Compensation means the system not causing the problem has moved its value in the opposite direction to push the pH back toward normal. If the other value is still normal, the imbalance is uncompensated; if it is abnormal in the compensating direction but the pH is still abnormal, it is partially compensated; if the pH has returned to 7.35–7.45 with both values abnormal, it is fully compensated. Students often miss the fully compensated result because the normal pH looks “fine,” but two abnormal values with a normal pH always mean full compensation.
questions.takeaway: Compensation is present whenever the non-causing value has moved abnormal in the opposite direction.
questions.hintContent: For each ABG, name the primary problem first, then check the other value.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply the same step-by-step routine to every option rather than eyeballing the pH.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client returned 2 hours ago from a bronchoscopy with biopsy performed under moderate sedation. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider immediately? Select all that apply.
options: A mild sore throat
SpO₂ falling from 96% to 89%
New sharp chest pain with a respiratory rate rising from 18 to 28/min
Small streaks of blood in the sputum after a biopsy
A high-pitched crowing sound on inspiration
optionRationales: Incorrect. A sore throat is expected after a scope passes through the throat.
Correct. A falling SpO₂ after the procedure signals a complication.
Correct. These findings suggest a pneumothorax from the biopsy.
Incorrect. Small blood streaks are expected after biopsy.
Correct. Stridor signals laryngeal swelling and upper airway obstruction.
questions.rationale: Bronchoscopy passes a scope into the airways to look inside, remove secretions, or take a biopsy. Afterward, a sore throat and small blood streaks in the sputum are expected. Stridor is a red flag for airway swelling, and new chest pain, rapid breathing, or a falling SpO₂ suggest complications such as a pneumothorax. The blood-streak option is tempting because blood usually sounds alarming, but small streaks after a biopsy are an expected finding.
questions.takeaway: After bronchoscopy, a sore throat and blood-streaked sputum are expected; stridor, chest pain, tachypnea, or falling SpO₂ are not.
questions.hintContent: Ask what normally follows a scope and biopsy, then look for anything beyond that.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate expected post-procedure findings from signs of a complication.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client’s pulse oximeter shows a weak, irregular waveform and an SpO₂ of 85%, yet the client is talking comfortably with pink oral mucosa. The client’s fingers are cold, and the client is wearing dark nail polish. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Tape the probe tightly to the finger to keep it in place
Correlate the reading with a respiratory assessment before acting on it
