Remove the nail polish from the monitored finger
Warm the client’s hand before rechecking
Increase the oxygen flow rate until the SpO₂ reaches 95%
Move the probe to an earlobe
optionRationales: Incorrect. Tight tape can reduce blood flow and further degrade the signal.
Correct. The nurse treats the client, not the number, and confirms with assessment.
Correct. Dark polish can block the light the oximeter uses.
Correct. Poor circulation to cold fingers causes a weak, inaccurate signal.
Incorrect. Changing oxygen in response to a likely inaccurate reading treats the device, not the client.
Correct. An alternate site can provide a better signal when finger perfusion is poor.
questions.rationale: Pulse oximetry estimates the percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen by shining light through tissue, and it has blind spots. Poor circulation to cold fingers, movement, and dark nail polish or artificial nails can all produce weak or inaccurate readings. When the number does not match how the client looks — talking comfortably with pink mucosa — the nurse fixes the sources of error, tries another site, and correlates with assessment. Turning up the oxygen is tempting because the number is low, but it treats a probably false reading rather than the client.
questions.takeaway: When the SpO₂ doesn’t match the client, fix the measurement and assess the client before changing therapy.
questions.hintContent: List what interferes with the light signal the oximeter depends on.
questions.hintStrategy: When assessment and a device conflict, choose actions that verify the device and assess the client.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a home asthma action plan with a client who is learning to use a peak flow meter. Which client statements indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “I only need to check my peak flow when I’m already very short of breath.”
“If my reading is 80% or more of my best, I keep following my usual plan.”
“If my reading is under 50%, I’ll wait an hour and check it again.”
“I compare each reading with my own personal best number.”
“If I’m between 50% and 79% of my best, I use my rescue inhaler and follow my action plan.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Regular readings help catch worsening early, before severe symptoms.
Correct. The green zone (≥ 80%) means good control.
Incorrect. The red zone (< 50%) is an emergency and needs immediate help, not waiting.
Correct. Peak flow zones are based on the client’s personal best, not on a population norm.
Correct. The yellow zone calls for rescue medicine and the action plan.
questions.rationale: A peak flow meter measures how fast the client can blow air out, and people with asthma use it at home to catch worsening early. Each reading is compared with the client’s personal best: green (80% or more) means continue the usual plan; yellow (50–79%) means use rescue medicine and follow the action plan; red (below 50%) is an emergency. Waiting to recheck a red-zone reading is the dangerous misunderstanding. Checking only when very short of breath defeats the purpose of early detection.
questions.takeaway: Peak flow zones: green ≥ 80%, yellow 50–79%, red < 50% of personal best — red means get help now.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three zones and the action tied to each.
questions.hintStrategy: For “indicates understanding” SATA items, test each statement against the rule — any delay in the red zone is wrong.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a pulmonary angiogram to evaluate a suspected clot. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Review the client’s serum creatinine before the procedure
Ask whether the client has ever reacted to contrast dye
After the procedure, check the catheter insertion site
Keep the client NPO after the procedure until the gag reflex returns
Position the client leaning forward over an overbed table for the procedure
optionRationales: Correct. The IV contrast dye can harm the kidneys, so kidney function is checked beforehand.
Correct. A prior contrast reaction must be reported to the provider before the study.
Correct. The catheter site is monitored for bleeding afterward.
Incorrect. This precaution applies after bronchoscopy, when the throat has been anesthetized.
Incorrect. This is the position used for thoracentesis, not angiography.
questions.rationale: A pulmonary angiogram uses IV contrast dye to show blood flow in the lung arteries, for example to find a clot. Before the test, the nurse checks kidney function and asks about previous reactions to contrast or dye, reporting any problems to the provider; afterward, the nurse checks the catheter site. The distractors borrow precautions from other tests: NPO until the gag reflex returns belongs to bronchoscopy, and leaning over an overbed table belongs to thoracentesis. Recognizing which precaution goes with which test is a common exam skill.
questions.takeaway: Contrast studies: check kidney function and contrast-reaction history before, and the catheter site after.
questions.hintContent: Identify what is injected during this test and which organs or sites it puts at risk.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that are correct for a different procedure.
